title: Design a Scalable Enterprise Frontend
description: Senior/lead system-design scenario covering domain boundaries, team ownership, dependency direction, lazy delivery, shared infrastructure and long-term maintainability.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Think of a large frontend as a set of owned business capabilities, not a pile of screens. The goal is to let teams change their own features without surprising other teams. Public APIs, one-way dependencies and lazy routes matter more than the exact folder names.

A modular monolith is often the best starting point because it keeps deployment and runtime simple while still allowing strong boundaries. Micro-frontends solve a narrower problem: separate ownership and release cadence at runtime. They add cost, so the reason for using them should be proven, not assumed.

Good architecture also needs feedback. CI rules, contracts, budgets and observability turn the design from a diagram into something the team can keep healthy over years.
keyPoints: Organize by business capability and ownership; expose explicit feature APIs and prohibit deep imports.
Prefer a modular monolith first. Add micro-frontends only for demonstrated independent-deployment or organizational needs.
Keep platform concerns shared, but keep feature rules, feature state and API orchestration owned by the feature.
Use typed API contracts, route-level lazy loading and clear state ownership.
Enforce architecture with CI dependency rules, code owners, contract tests, bundle budgets and observability.
Measure coupling and delivery outcomes, not only the visual folder structure.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: You are designing an Angular enterprise product with 40 screens, eight development squads, multiple APIs and a five-year lifetime. How would you structure the frontend?
blocks.answer:
I would start with business areas and team ownership, not folders like components and services. For an enterprise app, I want domains such as identity, payments, reporting, customer servicing and administration. Each domain gets an owner and a small public API. Other teams can use that API, but they cannot import private services, models or components from inside the feature.

My default shape would be a modular monolith. It is easier to build, test and operate than micro-frontends, and it still supports eight squads if the boundaries are real. Routes should be lazy loaded. Feature code can depend on platform utilities and the design system, but peer features should not depend on each other's internals.

Shared code should stay boring and platform-level: auth setup, config, telemetry, error handling, HTTP policies and design-system components. Business rules, workflow state and API orchestration stay inside the owning feature. I would avoid one global store and one shared services folder because they become unowned coupling points.

The API boundary is just as important as the UI boundary. I would use typed API contracts, generate or validate clients from OpenAPI where possible, and add a BFF only when aggregation, token isolation or frontend-specific payloads justify another service. Local UI state stays local, feature workflow state stays in the feature, URL state holds shareable filters, and server data is treated as remote cache.

Finally, the architecture needs enforcement. CI should check dependency rules, code owners, contract tests, bundle budgets, accessibility and important test gates. I would watch route size, cross-team change coupling, production error ownership and release coordination. If independent deployment becomes a real bottleneck later, then micro-frontends are worth evaluating.

blocks.explanation: Creating one huge shared module, one global store and a common services folder that every feature can modify. That appears reusable initially but becomes an unowned coupling point and makes independent change difficult.

blocks.title: Common weak answer
blocks.content: Creating one huge shared module, one global store and a common services folder that every feature edits. It looks reusable at first, but it becomes an unowned coupling point.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and production validation
blocks.content: A modular monolith is simpler to build, test and operate, but releases are still coordinated. Micro-frontends can give teams more autonomy, but they add runtime integration, duplicate dependencies, version drift and more observability work. Track route bundle sizes, cross-domain imports, change failure rate, cycle time and coordinated releases to know if the trade-off is paying off.
keyPoints: Production validation: Track route bundle sizes, cross-domain imports, change-failure rate, cycle time, production ownership and the number of coordinated releases required for ordinary feature changes.
Document the decision, assumptions, owner and rollback trigger so the architecture can be revisited when constraints change.

blocks.question: When would you move from a modular monolith to micro-frontends?
blocks.answer: I would move only when there is evidence: independently owned domains, a real need for separate release cadence, teams ready to operate their own runtime, and small integration contracts. First I would remove repo, build and pipeline bottlenecks. Micro-frontends should solve deployment autonomy, not weak modularity.
blocks.explanation: Micro-frontends are useful when organizational release independence is the main constraint, but they are not a shortcut for clean boundaries.

title: Domain Boundaries and Dependency Rules
description: How to divide a large frontend into business domains, prevent circular dependencies and make module boundaries enforceable.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Boundaries should follow ownership and change patterns. If two pieces of code usually change for different business reasons, they should not depend on each other's internals. A public API gives other teams something stable to use while preserving freedom inside the feature.

Dependency rules work best when they are simple and enforced automatically. Stop new deep imports first, then break the most painful cycles. Some duplication is acceptable if it keeps ownership clear.

Shared code needs a real owner and stable meaning. A neutral common folder without ownership is usually just a slower version of the same architectural problem.
keyPoints: Use business ownership and change patterns to define domains, not only technical file types.
Expose small public APIs and block deep imports into feature internals.
Define a one-way dependency graph and use an application orchestration layer for cross-domain workflows.
Stop new violations first, then migrate high-risk cycles incrementally.
Do not turn a shared/common library into a dumping ground for business logic.
Assign owners and compatibility rules to every cross-domain contract.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: Your repository has 2,000 components. Features import each other's services and internal models, circular dependencies are increasing, and every refactor breaks unrelated screens. How would you correct the architecture?
blocks.answer:
I would not start by moving thousands of files. First I would map the dependency graph and look at change history. Circular imports usually mean the system has unclear ownership or no agreed direction for dependencies.

Then I would group code by business capability. Reusable UI primitives belong in the design system, but business-specific components that only look similar should stay with the feature that owns the rule. Each domain should expose a small public entry point for contracts, routes or facades.

The dependency direction should be explicit. For example, the app shell can compose features, features can use their own data and domain code, and all of them can use platform and design-system libraries. A feature should not call another feature's private HTTP service or reducer. If two domains need to work together, orchestration belongs in the application layer or in a backend workflow API.

I would stop new violations first with lint or workspace rules. Then I would migrate the riskiest cycles in high-change areas, replace deep imports with public APIs, and move shared business rules to the domain that truly owns them. I would avoid creating a big common package because that often hides the same coupling under a new name.

Every cross-domain contract needs an owner, compatibility policy and deprecation path. Success is not just zero circular imports. The real test is whether one team can refactor inside a feature without making unrelated teams change code.

blocks.content: Strict boundaries can add small mapping code and a little duplication. That is usually better than shared mutable models that tie unrelated release decisions together. Use dependency checks, circular-import checks and change-coupling metrics to confirm refactors stay local.

blocks.question: What do you do when two features genuinely need the same business rule?
blocks.answer: Put the rule in the domain that owns the business concept and expose it through a stable contract. If the rule must be authoritative across systems, move it to a backend or domain service. I would create a neutral shared location only when ownership, lifecycle and meaning are truly common.
blocks.explanation: Shared business logic still needs a business owner, otherwise the shared layer becomes a dumping ground.

title: API Contracts and Backward Compatibility
description: Designing typed frontend/backend contracts, compatible evolution, deprecation, validation and mixed-version deployments.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
API compatibility is about mixed versions. In real products, several frontend builds, mobile clients and partners can be active at the same time. The contract must support that reality.

Prefer additive evolution because it lets old and new clients overlap. When a breaking change is unavoidable, run both paths for a while and remove the old one only after telemetry proves it is unused.

Types, schemas and contract tests reduce surprises, but they solve different problems. TypeScript improves developer safety; runtime validation and contract tests protect the deployed boundary.
keyPoints: Define the mixed-version compatibility window before choosing a versioning strategy.
Prefer additive changes and tolerant readers; do not silently change field meaning.
Use OpenAPI/schema review, generated clients, runtime validation for critical boundaries and contract tests.
Standardize machine-readable errors instead of parsing display messages.
Deploy breaking changes with expand -> migrate -> observe -> contract.
Measure deprecated endpoint usage before removal and preserve rollback compatibility.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: A backend team needs to change a customer API used by three frontend versions, mobile clients and a partner portal. How would you evolve the contract without breaking users?
blocks.answer:
I would treat the API contract as a product used by several clients, not as a backend detail. First I would define the compatibility window: old browser tabs, cached frontend assets, mobile app versions and partner clients may all live longer than one deployment.

The safest changes are additive. New optional fields, new endpoints and new enum values are easier to roll out than renaming fields or changing meaning in place. Clients should be tolerant readers where safe, but the API must not silently change semantics.

The contract should be machine-readable, usually OpenAPI or a similar schema, with examples and error behavior reviewed. Generated TypeScript helps developers, but it is not runtime validation. At important trust boundaries, I would validate critical payloads or fail safely when the shape is wrong. Contract tests should run before either side deploys.

For a breaking change, I would use expand, migrate, observe, contract. The backend supports old and new shapes, clients migrate and emit usage telemetry, the old form is deprecated with an owner, and only then is it removed. Versioned URLs or media types are useful when the meaning really changes, not for every additive field.

Errors need a stable shape too. The UI should use machine-readable error codes, not parse display text. The design is working when frontend and backend can deploy independently during the compatibility window and rollback still works.

blocks.explanation: Generating TypeScript interfaces and assuming the runtime response must match them. Types disappear at runtime, so a malformed or partially deployed response can still break the application.

blocks.code:
# Additive change: old clients continue to work
Customer:
  type: object
  required: [id, displayName]
  properties:
    id: { type: string }
    displayName: { type: string }
    riskCategory:
      type: string
      enum: [low, medium, high]
      nullable: true

# Error response follows a stable problem-details contract.
blocks.explanation: Adding an optional field is normally compatible, but clients must still handle unknown enum values and missing data. The schema should include examples and error semantics, not only field names.

blocks.content: Runtime validation improves safety but adds code and CPU cost, so use it at important external boundaries rather than every internal object. URL versioning is clear, but it can create many long-lived variants. Additive evolution is cheaper when the meaning stays compatible. Validate with contract tests, mixed-version canaries and telemetry by client build or API version.
keyPoints: Production validation: Run producer and consumer contract tests, canary mixed-version tests and telemetry by client build/API version. Confirm old clients still work before and after a rollback.
Document the decision, assumptions, owner and rollback trigger so the architecture can be revisited when constraints change.

blocks.question: How would you handle a backend enum that may gain new values?
blocks.answer: Add an explicit unknown fallback in the UI, keep the raw value for telemetry, and avoid runtime logic that throws on an unrecognized value. The API should document that the enum can grow, and the UI should show a safe generic state until it understands the new value.
blocks.explanation: Extensible enums let the backend evolve without crashing older clients.

title: Choosing REST, GraphQL or a BFF
description: Selecting an API interaction model based on data ownership, aggregation, caching, security, client diversity and operational cost.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
The choice is less about endpoint count and more about boundaries. REST is simple when resources match the UI. A BFF is useful when the frontend needs a secure composition layer. GraphQL is useful when clients need flexible queries and the organization can govern the schema.

Aggregation also changes failure behavior. One slow service should not always make the whole dashboard fail. Timeouts, partial responses and per-widget errors need to be designed explicitly.

Keep authority in the right place. A BFF can compose and secure frontend traffic, but domain services still own resource authorization and core business rules.
keyPoints: Choose from client diversity, aggregation needs, security boundaries, caching and organizational capability—not fashion.
Direct REST is simple when resources are client-friendly and browser access is acceptable.
A BFF can isolate tokens, aggregate services and return frontend-specific view models.
GraphQL requires schema governance, field authorization, query-cost limits and resolver observability.
Keep authoritative business rules in domain services, not in the BFF.
Design partial failure and timeouts explicitly for aggregated responses.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: A dashboard needs data from six services. Some teams propose GraphQL, others want direct REST calls, and security wants tokens kept out of browser JavaScript. What would you choose?
blocks.answer:
I would not choose GraphQL, REST or a BFF just because the dashboard talks to six services. I would first ask who owns the client experience, how many client types need different shapes, whether the browser may hold downstream tokens, what can be cached and where latency is coming from.

Direct REST is fine when the services already expose client-friendly resources and the browser is allowed to call them. It keeps HTTP caching simple and lets the browser parallelize independent requests. The cost is duplicated orchestration, more round trips and more backend topology leaking into the frontend.

Here, a BFF is likely attractive because security wants tokens out of browser JavaScript and the dashboard needs an aggregate view. The BFF can own the session, call downstream services, apply timeouts, normalize errors and return a frontend-shaped model. It should not become the place where core business rules live.

GraphQL is useful when many clients need flexible projections over a connected domain and the organization can run it well. That means schema ownership, field-level authorization, query-cost limits, caching strategy and resolver observability. It is not automatically faster; bad resolvers can move N+1 problems to the server.

For this case I would probably use Angular to BFF to services. If GraphQL later helps at the BFF or domain layer, I would add it for a specific reason. I would measure end-to-end latency, downstream fan-out, payload size, cacheability, partial failure behavior and ownership.

blocks.explanation: The BFF returns a client-focused view model and can represent optional widget failures without exposing internal service topology.

GraphQL gives flexible projections, but it raises operational and security complexity. Direct REST is simplest, but the client can become chatty and tightly aware of services. Measure latency, fan-out, timeout rates, payload size, cache hit rate and partial-failure behavior.
keyPoints: Production validation: Measure p50/p95 end-to-end latency, downstream fan-out, timeout rates, payload bytes, cache hit rate and whether one dependency failure degrades only the affected capability.
Document the decision, assumptions, owner and rollback trigger so the architecture can be revisited when constraints change.

blocks.question: Where should validation and authorization live in a BFF architecture?
blocks.answer: The BFF validates its own inputs and authorizes frontend-level capabilities. Downstream services still authorize access to their resources. A BFF should not become a trusted bypass around service authorization.
blocks.explanation: Defense in depth keeps each service responsible for the resources it owns.

title: Multi-Tenant Frontend Architecture
description: Designing tenant isolation, branding, runtime configuration, permissions, caching and observability for a SaaS frontend.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Multi-tenancy has two different concerns: presentation variation and data isolation. The browser can customize what the tenant sees, but it cannot be trusted to decide what the tenant may access.

Validated runtime config helps avoid a branch per customer. The risk is too many combinations, so the team needs supported profiles, schema checks and clear ownership.

Every cache, API call and telemetry path must respect tenant boundaries. One missing cache key or trusted client-supplied tenant ID can become a cross-tenant data leak.
keyPoints: Treat tenant configuration as presentation input, never as the authorization boundary.
Resolve tenant from a trusted server/session context and enforce tenant scope on every API operation.
Drive most variation through validated runtime config and design tokens, not forks per customer.
Centralize capability checks and avoid hard-coded tenant or role comparisons.
Partition private caches and telemetry to prevent cross-tenant leakage.
Test hostile tenant-ID manipulation, stale caches and cross-tab account switching.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: One Angular application serves 300 enterprise customers with different branding, feature entitlements, data regions and permissions. How would you design multi-tenancy safely?
blocks.answer:
I would separate tenant customization from tenant security. Branding, navigation and visible features can come from tenant configuration. Tenant isolation and authorization must come from the backend using the authenticated tenant context.

At startup, the app can resolve the tenant from a trusted hostname, route or server session, then load validated runtime configuration. That config can include design tokens, enabled modules, locale defaults and support links. It must not contain secrets, database identifiers or final authorization decisions.

The UI should ask capability questions like can approve payment, not compare hard-coded tenant names or roles. Most tenant variation should be handled through configuration, content and design tokens. Separate tenant-specific components should be rare because they multiply the test matrix.

Caches and telemetry must be tenant-aware. Private responses should not go into shared CDN caches, and client caches need keys that include user, tenant and other important variation. Logs can use pseudonymous tenant identifiers and should avoid PII. Data-region routing belongs at the edge, BFF or backend, not in an editable browser setting.

I would test tenant ID tampering, URL manipulation, stale caches, account switching across tabs and unsupported config combinations. The design is safe only when changing browser state cannot expose another tenant's data.

blocks.explanation: Runtime schema validation prevents a bad tenant configuration from crashing startup. The API still derives the authoritative tenant from the authenticated session.

blocks.content: Passing tenantId from localStorage on every request and assuming the backend can trust it, or creating a separate frontend branch for every customer.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and production validation
blocks.content: Configuration avoids code forks but creates many possible combinations. Limit supported profiles, validate config in CI and assign owners. Strong tenant isolation may reduce cache sharing, which is the right trade-off for private data. Validate with cross-tenant authorization tests, cache-key tests and data-region alerts.
keyPoints: Production validation: Run automated cross-tenant authorization tests, cache-key tests, configuration schema tests and production alerts for tenant mismatch or unexpected data-region routing.
Document the decision, assumptions, owner and rollback trigger so the architecture can be revisited when constraints change.

blocks.question: How would you prevent a shared CDN from serving tenant A's response to tenant B?
blocks.answer: Do not publicly cache private user responses. For cacheable tenant-specific public content, use explicit cache-control and a cache key that varies on the trusted tenant routing value. Verify the CDN setup with isolation tests, and never rely only on a client-supplied query parameter.
blocks.explanation: Shared caches are safe only when the cache key includes every trusted dimension that changes the response.

title: Architecture Decisions and Fitness Functions
description: Making architectural choices explicit, measurable and continuously enforceable instead of relying on slide decks.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
ADRs explain intent; fitness functions protect intent. A team can agree on lazy routes and no deep imports, but unless those rules are checked, daily delivery pressure will erode them.

Good architecture checks are important, measurable and hard to review manually every time. They should be fast, deterministic and tied to remediation guidance.

The process should allow learning. Baseline old debt, make exceptions visible and change the rule deliberately when constraints change.
keyPoints: Use ADRs to preserve context and reversal criteria; use automated fitness functions to enforce properties.
Automate dependency boundaries, bundle budgets, contract compatibility, security and quality gates.
Baseline existing debt and prevent regression instead of blocking all delivery immediately.
Make exceptions explicit, owned and expiring.
Review trends and outcomes, not only pass/fail checks.
Change the rule deliberately when constraints change; do not normalize silent bypasses.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: Your team agreed on lazy routes, no cross-feature imports and a 250 KB initial bundle budget, but six months later all three rules have been violated. How would you prevent architecture drift?
blocks.answer:
I would turn the architecture rules into checks the team can see and enforce. ADRs are useful for context: what decision was made, why, what alternatives were rejected, who owns it and when to revisit it. But documentation alone will not stop drift.

For each important property, I would add a fitness function. Dependency rules can fail deep imports and circular imports. Bundle budgets can be checked from production build stats. OpenAPI compatibility can be checked against the previous contract. Security headers, accessibility rules and critical journey performance can also be checked automatically.

I would not make hundreds of rules blocking on day one. Start with risks that are costly to reverse: domain coupling, API compatibility, security headers, bundle growth and unsupported browsers. Existing debt can be baselined so teams stop making it worse while they migrate.

Exceptions should be explicit, owned and time-bound. If a rule becomes wrong, update the ADR and the check. Do not let teams quietly bypass it until the rule means nothing.

Architecture review should use evidence. Track bundle trends, dependency violations, exception age, duplicated libraries, false positives and test reliability. The goal is to catch drift early, where it is cheap to fix.

# Example CI architecture gates
- run: npm run lint:boundaries
- run: npm run test:contracts
- run: npm run build -- --configuration production
- run: npm run check:bundle-budgets
- run: npm run test:a11y-critical
- run: npm run test:security-headers
blocks.explanation: These checks turn architecture into a property continuously verified on every change. The exact tools are less important than reliable, actionable feedback.

blocks.content: Blocking gates protect the system, but noisy gates create frustration. Keep checks fast, deterministic and linked to clear fixes. Some metrics should warn first, then become blocking after the baseline is understood. Track violations, exception age, false positives and time spent resolving checks.
keyPoints: Production validation: Track rule violations, exception age, bundle and dependency trends, false-positive rate and the time teams spend resolving architecture checks.
Document the decision, assumptions, owner and rollback trigger so the architecture can be revisited when constraints change.

blocks.question: What is a good candidate for a fitness function?
blocks.answer: A good fitness function checks a property that is important, measurable and easy to regress: no feature-to-feature deep imports, API backward compatibility, maximum initial bundle size, required CSP headers or a performance threshold for a critical journey. Subjective design quality still needs review, but repeatable properties should be automated.
blocks.explanation: Automating repeatable architecture checks catches drift earlier than manual review.

title: Build vs Buy and Third-Party Dependencies
description: Evaluating libraries and SaaS widgets using product fit, accessibility, security, performance, maintenance and exit strategy.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Build versus buy is a risk and ownership decision. Buy or adopt when the capability is hard, common and not your product's main differentiator. Build when the behavior is unique, narrow or strategically important.

A realistic POC is the best way to avoid surprise. Test scale, accessibility, security, theming and upgrade behavior before the dependency spreads.

The wider a dependency reaches, the more important a seam becomes. A small adapter can reduce future migration pain, but too much abstraction can become its own product.
keyPoints: Separate commodity capability from differentiating business behavior.
Evaluate accessibility, security, performance, licensing, maintainer health, upgrade cost and operational fit.
POC with real scale and edge cases, not vendor demo data.
Wrap high-impact dependencies behind a stable internal seam where replacement is plausible.
Include SaaS data handling, SLA, lock-in and exit terms.
Compare total lifecycle cost, not only purchase price or initial coding time.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: The team needs a data grid, rich-text editor and charting library. How would you decide whether to build, buy or adopt open source?
blocks.answer:
I would start by separating commodity capability from business differentiation. A full data grid with virtualization, keyboard support, pinned columns and export is expensive to build well. A simple company-specific card or workflow may be better owned directly by the team.

The evaluation should go beyond feature lists. I would check accessibility, performance at our real scale, framework and browser support, security history, maintainer health, licensing, bundle cost, theming, localization, SSR needs, testability and upgrade path. For paid tools, I would also review support, SLA, data handling, hosting region, lock-in and exit terms.

The proof of concept should use real edge cases. For a grid, that means large row counts, custom rendering, keyboard-only use, screen readers, dark and RTL themes, error states and production bundle analysis. Vendor demo data is not enough.

For high-impact dependencies, product code should go through an internal adapter or design-system component where practical. That gives a migration seam and keeps vendor APIs from spreading across hundreds of screens. The adapter should stay small; it should not try to hide every vendor feature.

The final decision should compare lifecycle cost, not just purchase price or first implementation speed. Open source still has upgrade, security and incident cost. Building gives control, but it also makes the team responsible for every browser, accessibility and maintenance issue.

blocks.content: An adapter improves replaceability but adds code and can hide useful vendor features. Use it for strategic or widely used dependencies, not every small utility. Building gives control but transfers accessibility, browser and maintenance work to your team. blocks.question: When should you reject a popular open-source dependency?
blocks.answer: Reject a popular dependency when it fails a hard requirement such as accessibility or security, is effectively unmaintained, has an incompatible license, adds unacceptable bundle or runtime cost, requires unsafe DOM bypasses, or exposes an API that would create hard-to-reverse coupling across the product.
blocks.explanation: Popularity does not offset a failed hard requirement or a dependency shape that the product cannot safely absorb.

title: Frontend Platform and Golden Path
description: Creating a paved road for teams: templates, CI, observability, security, design system, ownership and controlled extensibility.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
A good frontend platform reduces repeated decisions. Teams should not solve auth, logging, error handling and release setup eight different ways when secure defaults can be provided once.

The platform must be enabling, not controlling. Self-service tools and automated checks scale better than manual approval for ordinary work.

Treating the platform as a product keeps it honest. Adoption, upgrade pain and incident reduction are better signals than the number of packages published.
keyPoints: Provide secure, observable defaults through templates, generators and CI—not copy-paste documentation.
Keep platform contracts stable and focused; feature teams own business workflows.
Make the supported path easier than custom implementation.
Allow governed exceptions with owners and review dates.
Treat platform work as a product with adoption metrics, roadmap and migration support.
Prefer focused/build-time capabilities over a giant mandatory runtime package.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: Eight squads repeatedly solve authentication, API errors, logging, testing and release configuration differently. How would you create a frontend platform without slowing teams down?
blocks.answer:
I would create a paved road, not a review bottleneck. The platform should give squads secure and observable defaults through templates, generators and CI checks. That includes bootstrap config, identity, HTTP policies, normalized errors, telemetry, design-system setup, testing tools, lint rules, bundle budgets and deployment configuration.

The platform contract should be small and stable. It should own shared technical concerns, not product workflows. Feature teams still own domain state, business rules and release outcomes. A platform package that tries to own every decision becomes the new bottleneck.

Adoption comes from developer experience. Generators, examples, diagnostics, clear errors and migration guides make the supported path easier than custom work. Exceptions should be allowed when there is a real need, but they need an owner, review date and any required security review.

I would manage the platform like a product. Track usage, upgrade lag, duplicated security fixes, CI reliability, developer feedback and support load. Publish a roadmap and automate migrations where possible.

I would also avoid one giant mandatory runtime library. Prefer build-time tooling and focused packages so every app does not ship code it does not use.

title: Caching Strategy Across Browser, CDN and Client State
description: Layered caching for static assets, API responses and client query state with explicit freshness, privacy and invalidation rules.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Caching is not one policy. Assets, public reference data and private account data have different risk and freshness needs. The right cache lifetime comes from business meaning, not a global TTL.

HTTP caching should be used where it fits because the browser and CDN already understand validators and cache-control. Client caches are useful for UI state and server-state dedupe, but they need explicit invalidation and memory limits.

Freshness is part of correctness. Faster pages are not a win if they show another user's data or a stale balance that the business promised would be current.
keyPoints: Use content-hashed immutable caching for versioned assets and revalidate the app shell.
Prefer HTTP caching and validators before adding custom client caches.
Classify API data by sensitivity and acceptable staleness; never share-cache private responses.
Give every client cache entry a key, freshness, invalidation and eviction rule.
Invalidate dependent queries after mutations instead of clearing everything.
Measure hit rate and stale-data correctness, not only perceived speed.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: Your application loads slowly because the same assets and reference data are repeatedly downloaded, but customer balances must always be fresh. How would you design caching?
blocks.answer:
I would classify what is being cached by sensitivity and acceptable staleness. Static build assets are the easy case: hashed JavaScript, CSS, fonts and images can be cached for a long time as immutable. The app shell or index file should revalidate so it can find the latest asset hashes.

For API data, I would start with HTTP caching before building custom client caches. Public reference data can use Cache-Control, ETags and maybe a CDN. Private customer data needs private, no-store or short-lived policies and must never be stored in a shared cache. Cache keys need to vary on real dimensions such as locale, tenant or representation.

Inside Angular, I would use a bounded server-state cache to deduplicate requests and support stale-while-revalidate only where the business allows it. Every entry needs a key, freshness rule, invalidation rule, privacy classification and memory limit. Balances should be much fresher than product metadata.

After mutations, I would update the canonical entity and invalidate dependent summaries instead of clearing the entire app. Error responses should not be cached blindly. Offline storage is a separate decision because persisted data brings security, quota and migration concerns.

I would validate with transferred bytes, conditional requests, CDN and browser hit rates, stale-data incidents, memory growth, deployment behavior and account switching.

# Versioned assets

blocks.explanation: `no-cache` permits storage but requires revalidation; it does not mean the same thing as `no-store`. Hashed assets can be cached aggressively because a content change creates a new URL.

blocks.question: What is the difference between `no-cache` and `no-store`?
blocks.answer: no-cache allows a response to be stored, but it must be validated before reuse. no-store tells caches not to store the response at all. For sensitive data, choose based on the risk and product need; the names are not synonyms.
blocks.explanation: The key difference is that no-cache still permits storage while no-store forbids it.

title: Cache Invalidation and Stale Data
description: Maintaining consistent entity and derived-query caches after writes, external changes, reconnects and optimistic updates.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Stale UI often comes from duplicated ownership. Lists, details pages and suggestions should not each believe they own the same entity forever. Use stable IDs and update one canonical record when possible.

Invalidation should match the dependency. Rename may update entity views; status changes may also affect dashboard counts or filters. Broad cache clearing is simple but wasteful and still does not explain cross-user freshness.

Optimistic updates are a promise to reconcile later. They need rollback, ordering and conflict handling, especially when multiple editors or tabs are involved.
keyPoints: Use stable IDs and a canonical entity source instead of independent long-lived copies.
After mutation, update the authoritative entity and invalidate dependent lists, summaries and aggregates.
Return the server's canonical updated representation and version.
Optimistic updates require rollback/reconciliation and sequencing of conflicting writes.
Use ETag/version checks when lost updates matter.
Choose revalidation, polling or events based on the business freshness requirement.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: A user renames a vehicle. The details page updates immediately, but the dashboard and search suggestions continue to show the old name. How would you design consistency?
blocks.answer:
I would first define the canonical source for a vehicle. If the details page, dashboard and search suggestions each keep their own long-lived copy, stale data is expected. The UI needs stable IDs and one feature-level server-state cache or normalized store for the entity.

When the rename succeeds, the mutation should return the server's canonical updated vehicle and version. I would update that entity record, then invalidate or patch dependent queries. A list that shows the vehicle name may update from the entity; a dashboard count may need a refetch if the changed field affects aggregation.

Optimistic UI needs a clear rollback plan. I would capture the previous state, apply the temporary name, sequence or disable conflicting writes, then reconcile with the server response. If concurrent edits matter, ETag or version checks with If-Match let the server reject lost updates.

For changes from other users, the freshness model depends on the business need. Focus or reconnect revalidation may be enough for a display name. Polling or real-time versioned events may be needed for more critical data.

I would test rename then navigation, multiple tabs, rejected optimistic writes, delayed responses, offline reconnect and cross-user updates. The goal is not to avoid caching; it is to make ownership and staleness explicit.

blocks.question: How do you handle a `412 Precondition Failed` from `If-Match`?
blocks.answer: Fetch or use the server-provided latest representation, tell the user the record changed, and let them compare or reapply their edit. Do not silently overwrite the newer server state.
blocks.explanation: A 412 means the client's version is stale, so the user needs a safe conflict path.

title: Performance Investigation for a Large Dashboard
description: An evidence-led workflow for separating network, JavaScript, Angular rendering, DOM, layout, paint and third-party costs.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Performance work starts by separating causes. Startup bytes, API latency, rendering cost and main-thread CPU need different fixes. Guessing can easily move the bottleneck instead of removing it.

Dashboards should render progressively. The user should see the most important widgets quickly, while optional or expensive widgets load later with local failure states.

Optimization is only real when measured against the same journey. Field data matters because device class, browser and region often change the answer.
keyPoints: Profile before optimizing and separate network, bundle, API, Angular, DOM/layout and third-party costs.
Use representative devices and real-user data, not only a powerful development laptop.
Prioritize critical widgets; defer or lazy load expensive noncritical code and content.
Parallelize independent calls while preserving localized failure states.
Reduce repeated change detection, template computation and oversized DOM only where traces show cost.
Set measurable performance budgets and compare the same journey after every change.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: A dashboard with 30 widgets takes five seconds to become usable and occasionally freezes for two seconds. Walk through your investigation and redesign.
blocks.answer:
I would start with a profile, not a list of generic fixes. The five seconds could be network, JavaScript execution, auth bootstrap, API waterfalls, Angular rendering, layout work, charting code or third-party scripts. I would test on representative devices and networks, not only a fast laptop.

The network panel shows duplicated, sequential or blocked requests. A performance trace shows long tasks, layout and paint cost. Angular tooling can point to repeated change detection, expensive templates and lifecycle work. A bundle analyzer can show heavy libraries loaded too early. Real-user monitoring tells me which users are actually affected.

Then I would classify the 30 widgets. Critical above-the-fold widgets load first. Independent calls run in parallel with per-widget loading and error states. Heavy charts, editors and PDF tools are lazy loaded or deferred. Below-the-fold widgets load on viewport or interaction. Large lists are virtualized and stale requests are cancelled.

I would also check whether the API shape is hurting us. A BFF or batched endpoint can help if round trips and repeated orchestration dominate. But one giant endpoint can create head-of-line blocking and all-or-nothing failure, so grouping should follow criticality and ownership.

Every change needs a before and after number: first useful widget, LCP, INP, long-task time, bytes, API p95, DOM size and error rate. I would ship improvements incrementally and compare field metrics by build.

blocks.question: How would you decide whether to use a BFF for the dashboard?
blocks.answer: I would use traces to see whether browser round trips and repeated service orchestration dominate. A BFF is justified if it reduces latency, normalizes contracts or isolates tokens. I would still keep critical and optional data separable so one slow service does not delay the whole dashboard.
blocks.explanation: A BFF helps when composition or security is the bottleneck, but aggregation must not destroy progressive loading.

title: Bundle Size and Code Splitting
description: Reducing initial JavaScript without creating route waterfalls, duplicated dependencies or unusable deferred interactions.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Bundle size work is about when code is needed, not just how much code exists. Heavy tools should be loaded near the user action that needs them.

The build graph often reveals avoidable mistakes: duplicate packages, imports through barrels, side effects and dependencies referenced from shared modules. Fixing those can be safer than a large library migration.

Splitting shifts cost from startup to later interactions. That is good only when it matches real user journeys and does not create a waterfall.
keyPoints: Analyze production transfer and execution cost before changing dependencies.
Lazy load stable route/feature boundaries and dynamically import heavy minority-use tools.
Use direct imports and tree-shakable APIs; investigate duplicate versions and barrel side effects.
Do not replace a library only from package size—include correctness, maintenance and migration cost.
Avoid over-splitting and uncontrolled prefetch waterfalls.
Enforce initial/route budgets in CI and validate field startup performance.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: Your initial compressed JavaScript grows from 700 KB to 2.5 MB after adding charts, PDF export and an editor. What would you do?
blocks.answer:
I would inspect the production build graph first. Package size alone is not enough. I want compressed transfer, parse time, execute time and which routes actually use charts, PDF export and the editor.

The first split is usually at route or feature boundaries. Users should not download admin, reports, settings, charting and PDF code on the landing screen if they do not need it. In Angular, loadChildren, loadComponent and defer blocks can move heavy code off the initial path.

Then I would look for waste before replacing libraries. Duplicate versions, barrel imports with side effects, eager references and non-tree-shakable APIs can all bloat the initial bundle. If a huge library is used for one small utility, a native API or smaller package may be better, but correctness and maintenance matter.

Code splitting has costs. Too many tiny chunks can add request overhead and slow the first interaction that needs them. Prefetching everything also defeats the point. I would prefetch only high-probability next routes during idle time or after user intent.

Finally, I would add CI budgets for initial and critical route chunks with an explicit allowlist for deliberate growth. Success is faster usable startup, not simply more chunk files.

blocks.explanation: A defer block can split code only when the dependency is isolated from the eager graph.

title: Large Lists and Data Grids
description: Server-side query design, virtualization, stable selection, aggregation, export and accessibility for very large datasets.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Large grids are not just rendering problems. Filtering, sorting, totals and export are data problems, so the server must own them at million-row scale.

Virtualization helps the DOM, but it does not fix network, parsing or in-memory sorting of a huge dataset. Use it together with server-side querying.

Bulk selection is a semantic design issue. Select current page, selected IDs and all matching results are different behaviors and must be represented differently.
keyPoints: Keep filtering, sorting, pagination and aggregation server-side for very large datasets.
Use cursor or snapshot pagination when a changing dataset makes offsets unstable.
Virtualize rendered rows and use stable IDs with inexpensive templates.
Represent 'all matching' selection as query/snapshot plus exclusions.
Run exports as authorized asynchronous server jobs.
Test keyboard/screen-reader behavior and measure scroll, memory and stale-request handling.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: The backend contains one million transactions. Users need filtering, sorting, multi-select and export in an Angular grid. How would you design it?
blocks.answer:
I would treat the grid as a query UI over server-owned data. The browser should not download one million transactions and filter or sort them locally. The UI should keep a compact query model: filters, sort, visible columns, page size and cursor.

The server endpoint should be indexed and return a bounded page with only the fields needed. For changing datasets, cursor pagination is usually more stable than offsets, although numbered pages may require offsets or a snapshot token. Counts and aggregates should come from the server.

The grid should virtualize rendered rows so the DOM stays small. Row templates need to be cheap, IDs stable and selection independent from row object instances. Debounced inputs, cancellation and response ordering prevent old requests from overwriting newer results.

Selection needs precise product semantics. Normal selection can store IDs. Select all matching should store the query or snapshot ID plus exclusions, not a million IDs in memory. Export should be an authorized asynchronous server job using the same query and an authorization snapshot.

I would test keyboard and screen-reader behavior, scrolling, heap, stale request handling, selection under filter changes and export completion at realistic scale.

All matching selection should be tied to a server query or snapshot ID and should either reset or ask for confirmation when the query changes. Ambiguous selection is dangerous for bulk operations.
blocks.explanation: Bulk actions need clear selection semantics so users do not act on the wrong records.

title: Main-Thread CPU, Long Tasks and Web Workers
description: Keeping interactions responsive when parsing, transforming, compressing or calculating large datasets.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Long tasks block input because the browser's main thread is doing too much. Workers help when the work is pure computation and can communicate through messages.

Before adding a worker, make the work smaller and better. Moving inefficient code to another thread can hide the symptom while increasing memory and complexity.

Backend jobs are the right answer when the browser is the wrong authority or the data is too large. The interview trade-off is UI responsiveness, total time, security and operational cost.
keyPoints: Profile and optimize the algorithm/input before introducing a worker.
Use workers for pure CPU work that does not require the DOM.
Define typed request IDs, progress, cancellation and error messages.
Account for structured-clone/transfer cost and memory duplication.
Use backend jobs when authority, scale or security exceeds browser limits.
Measure main-thread responsiveness and total completion time separately.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: Generating a risk report freezes the page for three seconds while JavaScript parses and aggregates data. How would you redesign it?
blocks.answer:
I would first profile the report generation to confirm the freeze is CPU work on the main thread. A worker will not fix a bad algorithm; it only moves suitable work away from rendering and input handling. I would reduce input size, remove repeated transformations and choose a better algorithm if needed.

A Web Worker is a good fit for pure CPU work that does not need the DOM: parsing, aggregation, compression or heavy calculations. I would define typed messages with request IDs, progress, cancellation and error responses.

Large data transfer matters. Structured cloning can copy a lot of memory and time. For large binary data, transferable ArrayBuffers or chunked processing may be better. The worker should be lazy loaded so users who never run the report do not pay for it.

The main thread should own UI state, progress display and cancellation. It should ignore late results from cancelled jobs and keep interactions responsive. If the calculation must be authoritative, security-sensitive or too large for browser memory, I would use an async backend job instead.

I would measure long tasks, INP, worker startup, total job time, transfer time, memory on both sides, cancellation latency and result correctness. Responsiveness and total completion time are separate success measures.

blocks.explanation: Chunking is useful when the overhead of a worker is larger than the work itself.

title: Large File Upload, Download and Streaming
description: Designing resumable transfers, progress, integrity, memory safety and asynchronous server processing.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Large files fail when they are treated like small JSON requests. The browser needs resumable chunks, bounded memory and explicit progress. The server needs session state, integrity checks and cleanup.

Transfer completion is not the same as business readiness. A file can upload successfully and still fail malware scanning or schema validation. The UI should show that lifecycle clearly.

Direct object storage can reduce app-server load, but only if the signed authorization is narrow and the backend verifies the completed object before use.
keyPoints: Use resumable chunked upload sessions; do not load multi-gigabyte files into memory.
Separate transfer completion from scanning, validation and business processing.
Limit chunk concurrency and report server-confirmed progress.
Use range-capable server/object-storage downloads with short-lived authorization.
Enforce server-side type, size, content and malware checks.
Design idempotent finalize, session expiry and abandoned-part cleanup.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: Users upload 5 GB reconciliation files and download multi-gigabyte exports over unreliable networks. A normal browser request frequently fails or exhausts memory. What architecture would you use?
blocks.answer:
I would separate file transfer from file processing. For upload, the browser creates an upload session with metadata, allowed type, size and authorization. The file is then sent in bounded chunks with an upload ID, part numbers or byte ranges and integrity checks.

The browser should never load the full 5 GB file into memory. It should slice the File object, limit concurrency and retry failed chunks without restarting from byte zero. Progress should be based on bytes confirmed by the server, not just bytes handed to the network stack.

After transfer, scanning, schema validation and business processing happen on the server as a separate asynchronous job. The server must not trust file names, MIME types or client-side validation. It should store uploads safely, enforce quotas and clean up abandoned parts.

For downloads, I would prefer a generated object with a short-lived authorized URL and HTTP range support so downloads can resume. If the app must transform data client-side, streams and incremental writes are better than building one huge Blob, but browser support may require a simpler server-side path.

The design needs idempotent finalization, session expiry, duplicate handling and authorization checks. I would test network loss, tab close and reopen, duplicate chunks, checksum failure, quota exhaustion, malicious files and expired authorization.

blocks.question: How would you secure a direct-to-storage upload?

title: Image, Font and Media Performance
description: Choosing formats, responsive sources, priority, lazy loading, dimensions, font strategy and CDN transformations.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Media performance is about priority and fit. The browser should download the smallest asset that looks good at the rendered size, and it should discover critical assets early.

Lazy loading is good for noncritical media but bad for the LCP image. Preloading is powerful but can hurt when the wrong resource gets priority.

Fonts and images can also cause layout shifts. Reserving dimensions and controlling fallback font metrics are part of the design, not polish at the end.
keyPoints: Find the real LCP and CLS causes before changing all assets.
Serve responsive, right-sized, compressed images with stable dimensions.
Prioritize the LCP image; lazy load only noncritical media.
Budget and subset fonts; preload only truly critical resources.
Use streaming/facades for heavy video and third-party embeds.
Measure field LCP, CLS, transferred bytes, decode time and cache behavior.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: A content-heavy portal has a poor LCP and large layout shifts because hero images, thumbnails and custom fonts load inefficiently. How would you redesign delivery?
blocks.answer:
I would first identify the real LCP element and the sources of layout shift from field data and lab traces. Then I would optimize the assets that matter instead of changing every image and font blindly.

For images, the server or image CDN should serve right-sized variants. Responsive srcset and sizes, modern formats where supported, sensible compression and explicit width and height or aspect ratio reduce bytes and prevent layout movement.

The LCP image should not be lazy loaded. It should be discoverable early, prioritized correctly and not hidden behind a late JavaScript callback. Below-the-fold images can use native lazy loading with placeholders that reserve space. Angular's optimized image tools can help, but I would still verify the network behavior.

Fonts need a budget. I would subset character ranges, reduce weights and styles, preload only the critical font, use font-display deliberately and choose fallback metrics that avoid large reflow. Self-hosting gives more control and privacy; a CDN may help distribution depending on policy.

Large video and embeds should not block startup. Use streaming or adaptive delivery, poster images and facade loading for third-party embeds. I would measure field LCP, CLS, transferred bytes, decode time, font timing, cache hit rate and mobile data use.

blocks.answer: Preload gives a resource high priority. If that resource is not needed immediately, it competes with critical CSS, JavaScript and the true LCP resource. I would preload only assets proven to be on the critical path.

title: Memory Leaks and Long-Running Sessions
description: Finding retained components, subscriptions, DOM nodes, caches, event listeners and third-party resources in enterprise SPAs.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
A memory leak is about retained reachability, not just high memory. The key question is what still points to old objects after the user leaves the route.

Long-running dashboards stress lifecycle mistakes. Subscriptions, listeners, timers, charts, workers and caches all need clear owners and cleanup rules.

Some memory growth is intentional caching. That still needs a budget, eviction policy and account or tenant boundaries.
keyPoints: Use repeatable navigation loops and heap snapshots to find retained object paths.
Distinguish temporary allocation, intentional cache growth and true leaks.
Clean up every externally created resource: subscriptions, listeners, timers, workers, charts and observers.
Scope services/state appropriately and bound caches by size and time.
Prefer managed singleton real-time connections over per-component connections.
Verify memory returns after the same workflow and monitor long sessions in production.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: An operations dashboard remains open for an entire shift. Memory grows from 200 MB to 1.5 GB and the page becomes slow after several route changes. How would you investigate?
blocks.answer:
I would create a repeatable reproduction first. The dashboard should run through the same route changes, dialogs and refresh cycles while I record heap, DOM node counts and performance. One high heap number is not enough; I need to know whether memory returns after garbage collection.

Heap snapshots and allocation timelines can show what is retained. I would look for detached DOM nodes, old component instances, chart objects, timers, event listeners, observers, workers and cached responses. The retained path matters because it tells us who is still holding the object.

In Angular, common causes include manual subscriptions that outlive components, root services holding component callbacks, unbounded shareReplay or Maps, repeated event registration and third-party widgets that are not destroyed. takeUntilDestroyed helps with subscriptions, but it does not clean up every external resource or bound cache.

The fix should follow ownership. Whoever creates a timer, listener, observer, worker, chart or connection owns its cleanup. Feature state should not accidentally become root state. Caches need TTL or size limits and should clear on logout or tenant switch. Real-time connections should usually be managed as shared singletons, not created per component render.

After each fix, I would rerun the exact loop and compare retained objects. Production telemetry for long sessions can catch issues that local tests miss. I would also distinguish true leaks from intentional cache growth that simply exceeds the memory budget.

title: Edge/CDN Delivery and Network Resilience
description: Static delivery, cache keys, compression, origin shielding, timeouts, retries and graceful behavior on slow or unstable networks.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
CDNs are excellent for immutable assets and risky for private data unless the cache policy is exact. Treat those paths separately.

Network resilience is not infinite retry. It is safe retry for the right operations, clear failure states and recovery on reconnect.

Regional performance needs measurement by geography and phase. A slow page could be DNS, TLS, edge, origin, API fan-out or client execution.
keyPoints: Cache immutable static assets at the edge and revalidate the app shell.
Treat private/API caching separately and verify every cache-key variation.
Use compression, regional routing and origin shielding where measurements justify them.
Retry only transient safe/idempotent operations with limits, backoff and jitter.
Provide localized failure and reconnection behavior instead of infinite spinners.
Use RUM by region to distinguish network, edge and origin latency.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: Users in several regions experience slow startup and intermittent API failures. The application is hosted in one region. How would you improve delivery without serving stale or private data incorrectly?
blocks.answer:
I would split static delivery from dynamic data. Hashed frontend assets should be compressed, cached immutably at the edge and kept available during deployment rollouts. The app shell should stay small and revalidate so it can discover the current asset versions.

Private API data needs a different policy. I would not put user-specific responses in a shared CDN cache unless the platform has a proven private-cache design. Authorization, cookies, tenant, locale and query parameters can all affect whether a response is shareable. Missing one cache-key dimension can become a data leak.

For regional latency, I would use measurements before changing topology. Regional routing, origin shielding or a BFF closer to users may help, but only if data residency and downstream services support it. Compression and connection reuse can also matter.

Retries should be limited and intentional. The frontend can retry transient failures for safe or idempotent operations with backoff and jitter. It should not blindly retry payments or authorization failures. The UI should show local errors, reconnect states or read-only fallbacks where the business allows them.

I would use RUM by region to separate DNS, TLS, connection time, TTFB, transfer and server time. Synthetic tests help availability, but field data tells us what users actually feel. The goal is to put reusable bytes close to users without breaking freshness or privacy.

blocks.question: Should the frontend retry a failed POST automatically?
blocks.answer: Only if the operation is explicitly idempotent through its semantics or an idempotency key, and the error is transient. Otherwise an automatic retry can duplicate a payment or order. Retry behavior should be part of the API contract.
blocks.explanation: Unsafe POST retries can repeat side effects unless the operation is designed for idempotency.

title: Authentication with OIDC/OAuth for Browser Applications
description: Choosing OIDC/OAuth flows and SPA/BFF architectures while protecting redirects, tokens, sessions and logout.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
OIDC answers who the user is; API authorization answers what the user may do. A route guard can improve UX, but it does not secure a resource.

Browser apps are public clients. They cannot keep client secrets, so PKCE and exact redirect validation are required in a pure SPA.

For high-value systems, keeping tokens out of JavaScript with a BFF often improves the threat model. It shifts complexity to server sessions and CSRF handling, so it must be designed deliberately.
keyPoints: Delegate credentials to an OIDC provider; do not build authentication forms and password handling in the SPA.
Use Authorization Code with PKCE for browser public clients.
Consider a BFF with HttpOnly session cookies to keep OAuth tokens out of browser JavaScript.
Validate redirect URI, state, PKCE and nonce; never embed a client secret.
Keep access short-lived and least-privileged; design renewal, logout and step-up authentication.
Authenticate once but authorize every protected API operation.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: How would you design enterprise SSO for an Angular application that accesses high-value banking APIs?
blocks.answer:
I would not build username and password handling inside Angular. The app should delegate authentication to the enterprise OpenID Connect provider and use maintained, standards-based client or BFF libraries.

For a pure SPA, the correct modern flow is Authorization Code with PKCE. The browser is a public client, so it must not contain a client secret. Redirect URIs must be exact and allowlisted, and state, PKCE and nonce must be tied to the login transaction and validated.

For high-value banking APIs, I would strongly consider a BFF. The BFF completes the code exchange, keeps OAuth tokens server-side and gives the browser a Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite-aware session cookie. The browser calls the BFF, and the BFF applies CSRF defenses and forwards authorized requests.

A BFF reduces token theft through JavaScript, but it does not make XSS harmless. Malicious script can still act as the user from the trusted origin. Strong output handling, CSP, Trusted Types and sensitive-action reauthentication remain important.

Authentication is only the start. Every protected API operation must authorize the subject, tenant, resource and action. I would design token lifetime, renewal, logout, revocation, multi-tab behavior, session timeouts and step-up authentication for sensitive actions.

blocks.question: What can an attacker do if XSS occurs even when tokens are in HttpOnly cookies?
blocks.answer: The attacker may not be able to read the cookie, but script running in the origin can issue authenticated requests and manipulate the UI. HttpOnly reduces credential exfiltration; it does not make XSS harmless. Strong output handling, CSP, Trusted Types and sensitive-action reauthentication still matter.
blocks.explanation: HttpOnly protects token secrecy, not the integrity of actions made by malicious same-origin script.

title: Token and Session Storage
description: Evaluating memory, Web Storage and HttpOnly cookie designs based on XSS, CSRF, persistence, multi-tab behavior and operational constraints.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
The core issue is bearer-token exposure. If script can read the token, XSS can steal it. If a cookie is HttpOnly, script cannot read it, but the browser can still send it automatically.

No browser storage option eliminates compromise. Each option moves risk between persistence, exfiltration, CSRF and operational complexity.

A strong answer connects storage to session lifecycle: renewal, logout, revocation, account switching, cache clearing and server-side authorization.
keyPoints: JavaScript-readable storage cannot protect bearer tokens from same-origin malicious script.
HttpOnly cookie/BFF designs reduce token exfiltration but require CSRF-aware session handling.
Memory storage reduces persistence but does not defeat active XSS and complicates refresh.
Use short-lived, scoped credentials and provider-supported rotation/revocation.
Never put tokens in URLs, logs, analytics or error reports.
Clear user-specific caches and synchronize logout/account switching across tabs.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: Where should an Angular application store access and refresh tokens, and what trade-offs would you explain in an interview?
blocks.answer:
I would explain that token storage is a threat-model decision, not a single best practice. Any bearer token readable by JavaScript can be stolen by malicious JavaScript running in the same origin. localStorage, sessionStorage and IndexedDB have different persistence, but none protects against XSS.

Memory storage reduces persistence, but it does not defeat active XSS in the running page. It also complicates refresh and multi-tab behavior. Tokens should never go in URLs, logs, analytics or error reports because they leak easily.

For sensitive enterprise apps, I often prefer a BFF or server session. OAuth tokens stay on the server. The browser gets a Secure, HttpOnly cookie with an appropriate SameSite setting. JavaScript cannot read it, which reduces token exfiltration.

Cookie sessions require CSRF-aware design because browsers attach cookies automatically. The backend needs CSRF tokens, Origin or Fetch Metadata checks where appropriate, and server-side authorization on every operation. XSS still matters because malicious script can send authenticated requests.

If a pure SPA must hold an access token, I would use Authorization Code with PKCE, short-lived and least-privileged tokens, provider-supported renewal or rotation, minimal persistence and strong XSS prevention. Logout, account switching and tenant switching must clear user-specific caches and synchronize across tabs.

blocks.question: Is `sessionStorage` safe for access tokens?
blocks.answer: sessionStorage is less persistent and scoped to one tab, but it is still JavaScript-readable and vulnerable to XSS in that tab. I would not call it secure storage; I would describe its narrower persistence trade-off.

title: Authorization: RBAC, Permissions and ABAC
description: Designing capability-based UI behavior while keeping resource authorization authoritative on the server.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
RBAC works well for coarse assignment, but real products often need attributes too: region, ownership, amount and resource state. That is where ABAC or policy evaluation becomes important.

The frontend should use capabilities because they map to product actions and keep role names out of components. The server remains authoritative because it has trusted resource data and cannot be bypassed by edited browser state.

Filtering unauthorized data at the API is as important as blocking actions. Hiding a button is user guidance, not security.
keyPoints: Use capability checks instead of hard-coded role-name comparisons.
Server-side authorization is authoritative for every resource and operation.
Filter unauthorized data at the API; do not rely on UI hiding.
Use RBAC for coarse assignment and attributes/resource context where rules require it.
Treat permissions, feature flags and authentication as separate concepts.
Test horizontal/vertical escalation, stale policy and direct API manipulation.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: An application supports admins, approvers, branch users and external auditors. Permissions also depend on account ownership, region and transaction amount. How would you design authorization?
blocks.answer:
I would separate the frontend experience from the security decision. The UI needs enough information to hide, disable or explain actions, but the backend must authorize every resource and operation because browser requests can be changed.

I would avoid role-name checks scattered through templates. Instead, the app should ask capability questions such as can approve payment with context. Roles can be one input, but the effective policy may also depend on account ownership, region, tenant, amount or time.

For context-heavy rules, the server should evaluate the authoritative resource state. The frontend can make a preliminary decision for usability, but it must handle a later 403 if policy or resource state changed.

List APIs should not send unauthorized records and rely on the UI to hide them. APIs should filter data by subject, tenant and resource policy. Sensitive actions may require step-up authentication, maker-checker separation and audit records.

Permissions, feature flags and authentication are different. Login says who the user is. Permissions say what they can do. Feature flags control rollout. I would test vertical escalation, horizontal access, direct API calls, stale permission data and object ID manipulation.

blocks.question: What should the UI do after the API returns 403 for an action it showed as allowed?

title: XSS, CSP and Trusted Types
description: Preventing injection through safe rendering, contextual handling, sanitization and browser-enforced defense in depth.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Safe rendering starts with context. Text should be escaped as text. HTML needs sanitization because the browser will interpret tags, attributes and URLs.

Framework bypass APIs are dangerous because they remove protections. They should be rare, reviewed and tied to a trusted source, not used to preserve formatting from untrusted input.

CSP and Trusted Types reduce blast radius and catch unsafe patterns, but they do not replace safe output handling and sanitization.
keyPoints: Use normal framework text/template binding for untrusted text.
Prefer structured content or limited Markdown over arbitrary HTML.
Sanitize rich content with an allowlist and avoid broad trust-bypass APIs.
Inventory dangerous DOM sinks and dynamic URL/script creation.
Use strict CSP and Trusted Types as defense in depth.
Include third-party scripts and rich-content pipelines in security testing.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: The product must display comments and rich HTML imported from external systems. Developers are using `innerHTML` and Angular bypass APIs. How would you redesign it?
blocks.answer:
I would first reduce the amount of rich HTML we accept. Plain comments should render through Angular interpolation or text bindings so the framework escapes them. If the product can use structured content or limited Markdown instead of arbitrary HTML, that is safer and easier to reason about.

When HTML is truly required, I would define a reviewed trust boundary. Content should be sanitized with an allowlist for the needed tags, attributes and URL schemes. Stored content may be sanitized on the server, and rendering should still use Angular's supported sanitization path because contexts can change.

I would not fix this by calling bypassSecurityTrustHtml broadly. That tells Angular to trust the value; it does not make the value safe. Dangerous sinks such as innerHTML, outerHTML, document.write, dynamic script URLs, event-handler attributes and unsafe URL construction should be inventoried and routed through reviewed helpers.

CSP and Trusted Types are defense in depth. I would start CSP in report-only mode, then move toward a strict nonce or hash policy. Trusted Types can force dangerous DOM sinks through approved policies in browsers that support it.

Third-party scripts belong in the threat model because they run with page privileges. I would minimize them, load them only where needed and avoid putting sensitive values in the DOM. Testing should include stored, reflected and DOM XSS payloads, encoded variants, SVG and URL scheme cases, sanitizer regressions and CSP reports.

blocks.question: Why is escaping not enough for arbitrary rich HTML?
blocks.answer: Escaping turns markup into text, which is safe but does not preserve formatting. If markup must be rendered, it needs context-aware sanitization that removes dangerous elements, attributes and URL schemes. Marking raw HTML trusted skips that protection.
