title: CSRF, CORS and SameSite
description: Understanding origin policy, cookie-based request forgery and layered server/client defenses.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
CORS, CSRF and SameSite solve different problems. CORS is about cross-origin browser access. CSRF is about unwanted requests with automatically attached credentials. SameSite reduces some cross-site cookie sending, but it is not a complete payment defense.

A CSRF token works because the attacker can cause a request but cannot normally read same-origin token data or set approved custom headers. The server must validate it.

Cookie-based sessions need CSRF controls, while bearer headers have different risks around token theft and XSS.
keyPoints: CORS is a browser read/request policy, not API authentication or authorization.
CSRF matters when credentials are attached automatically, especially cookies.
Use SameSite as defense in depth, not the only protection for sensitive writes.
Use framework-supported CSRF tokens and consider Origin/Fetch Metadata validation.
Allow exact trusted origins for credentialed CORS; never use wildcard.
Prevent XSS because same-origin malicious script can defeat CSRF protections.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: An Angular BFF uses HttpOnly session cookies. The team says CORS and `SameSite=Lax` are enough to prevent forged payments. Are they correct?
blocks.answer:
No, CORS and SameSite=Lax are not enough by themselves for forged payments. CORS controls whether browser JavaScript from another origin can read or make certain credentialed cross-origin requests. It is not authentication, and it does not stop non-browser clients.

CSRF matters when the browser attaches credentials automatically, such as cookies. An attacker page may be able to trigger a state-changing request even though it cannot read the response. Sensitive writes like payments need more than a broad SameSite assumption.

SameSite is useful defense in depth, but the correct setting depends on login flows, browser behavior and same-site subdomain risk. The backend should use a framework-supported CSRF design, such as a synchronizer token or signed double-submit pattern, and may also validate Origin and Fetch Metadata. State-changing operations should not use GET.

For Angular with a same-origin BFF, the server can issue a readable XSRF token cookie while keeping the session cookie HttpOnly. Angular echoes the token in a custom header. An attacker site can send the cookie, but normally cannot read the token or set the approved custom header because of same-origin and CORS rules.

Credentialed CORS should allow only exact trusted origins, never wildcard. XSS can bypass CSRF protections by running in the trusted origin, so output handling and CSP still matter. I would test forged forms, simple content types, invalid tokens, trusted and untrusted origins, sibling subdomains and every state-changing method.

blocks.code:
Set-Cookie: __Host-session=...; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax
Set-Cookie: XSRF-TOKEN=random; Secure; SameSite=Lax

POST /bff/payments
Cookie: __Host-session=...
X-XSRF-TOKEN: random
Origin: https://app.example.com
blocks.explanation: The session credential remains unreadable to JavaScript, while the CSRF token is echoed in a custom header and validated by the server.

blocks.title: Common weak answer
blocks.content: Enabling Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * and believing it secures the API, or relying on SameSite alone for irreversible financial operations.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and production validation
blocks.content: Token validation and origin checks add coordination, but they protect cookie sessions. Strict SameSite reduces CSRF exposure but may break legitimate identity or cross-site flows. Choose deliberately and test cross-site forms, credentialed fetches, missing tokens, Origin and Fetch Metadata checks, subdomain assumptions and all state-changing methods.
keyPoints: Production validation: Test cross-site forms, credentialed fetches, missing/wrong tokens, Origin/Fetch Metadata, subdomain takeover assumptions and every state-changing method.
Document the decision, assumptions, owner and rollback trigger so the architecture can be revisited when constraints change.

blocks.question: Does a bearer token in an `Authorization` header eliminate CSRF?
blocks.answer: It reduces traditional cookie-based CSRF because browsers do not attach the Authorization header automatically. However, token theft, XSS and client-side request construction remain concerns. Security still depends on how the token is obtained and stored.
blocks.explanation: Bearer headers avoid automatic cookie attachment, but they do not solve token compromise or malicious same-origin script.

title: Frontend Security Threat Modeling
description: Mapping assets, actors, entry points, trust boundaries and abuse cases before implementation.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Threat modeling is structured thinking before controls are chosen. Start with assets, actors, entry points and trust boundaries, then turn them into concrete abuse cases.

The best models are specific to the product. A payment approval flow has different risks than a marketing page, so the controls should connect to payments, files, identity, notifications and third-party code.

The output should be actionable: requirements, tests, monitoring, owners and accepted residual risk. A long generic document is less useful than a focused model tied to the architecture.
keyPoints: Identify assets, actors, entry points and trust boundaries before choosing controls.
Model browser, identity, API, storage, real-time and third-party flows.
Write concrete abuse cases such as IDOR, replay, malicious upload and cross-tenant events.
Prioritize by business impact and attack feasibility.
Convert threats into owned requirements, tests, telemetry and residual-risk decisions.
Revisit the model whenever data flows or trust assumptions change.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: You are designing a payment approval frontend with file upload, third-party analytics, OIDC login and real-time notifications. How would you threat-model it?
blocks.answer:
I would start by drawing the system and data flows. The assets include the session, payment instructions, PII, approval authority, uploaded files and audit records. Actors include normal users, malicious users, compromised accounts, attacker-controlled sites, third-party scripts and internal services.

Then I would mark trust boundaries: browser, identity provider, BFF, APIs, object storage, notification channel and external vendors. For each flow, I would ask what can be spoofed, tampered with, disclosed, replayed or denied.

Concrete abuse cases matter more than a generic checklist. Examples are redirect manipulation during login, CSRF payment submission, XSS through payee names, IDOR by changing payment IDs, malicious upload previews, WebSocket subscriptions to another user's events and analytics receiving PII.

I would prioritize by business impact and attack feasibility. High-value controls might include server-side authorization, maker-checker approval, step-up authentication, authoritative transaction confirmation, idempotency, replay protection, secure sessions, strict content handling, upload quarantine and scoped real-time subscriptions.

Threats should become owned requirements, tests, telemetry and residual-risk decisions. I would record assumptions, such as trusted devices or same-site subdomains, and revisit the model whenever a new integration or data flow appears.

blocks.code:
Attacker site -> Browser [CSRF / clickjacking]
Third-party script -> DOM/session actions [supply-chain/XSS]
Browser -> BFF [session + CSRF boundary]
BFF -> Payment API [authorization + idempotency]
Browser -> Upload storage [malicious file / scope]
Notification service -> Browser [tenant/topic authorization]
blocks.explanation: The diagram highlights separate trust boundaries. Each arrow needs authentication, authorization, validation, confidentiality, failure and logging decisions.

blocks.title: Common weak answer
blocks.content: Running a scanner at the end and calling that threat modeling, or listing the OWASP Top 10 without connecting threats to the actual payment flow.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and production validation
blocks.content: Threat modeling takes effort, so focus first on high-value flows and meaningful changes. Avoid both extremes: a ceremonial 100-page document and no structured security design. Track unresolved high-risk threats, abuse-case test coverage, security telemetry, third-party changes and incident learnings.
keyPoints: Production validation: Track unresolved high-risk threats, test coverage for abuse cases, security-control telemetry, third-party/data-flow changes and incident learnings.
Document the decision, assumptions, owner and rollback trigger so the architecture can be revisited when constraints change.

blocks.question: What special risk does a third-party analytics script create?
blocks.answer: It runs with the page's JavaScript privileges and may read DOM data or perform authenticated actions. I would minimize data exposure, load it only where needed, review vendor and change controls, apply CSP, SRI or sandboxing where possible, and never place sensitive values in easy-to-scrape DOM attributes.
blocks.explanation: Third-party analytics code can become part of your trusted computing base inside the browser.

title: Third-Party Script and Software Supply-Chain Security
description: Controlling npm dependencies, remote scripts, integrity, privileges, updates, SBOM and incident response.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Third-party JavaScript expands your trusted computing base. A script tag is not just an integration point; it is code running with page privileges.

Supply-chain risk includes both runtime scripts and build-time dependencies. A clean vulnerability scan today does not prove the package, maintainer or future update is safe.

Risk can be reduced with isolation, pinning, CSP, lockfiles, inventory, adapters and a rapid disable path. The amount of control should match the sensitivity of the workflows the code can touch.
keyPoints: Treat third-party JavaScript as same-origin privileged code.
Prefer server/API integration or sandboxed isolation where browser execution is unnecessary.
Pin immutable scripts with SRI where applicable and restrict sources through CSP.
Review transitive dependencies, install scripts, licensing, maintainers and update policy.
Maintain lockfiles, inventory/SBOM, rapid disable capability and an exit plan.
Design graceful failure so a vendor outage does not break critical journeys.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: A fraud analytics vendor asks you to paste a remote `<script>` tag into every page. The package also brings 80 transitive npm dependencies. What would you evaluate?
blocks.answer:
I would treat the vendor script as privileged application code. Once it runs on our page, it may read DOM content, observe inputs, send network requests and perform authenticated actions. The first questions are what data it needs, where it sends it, how code changes are released and whether the business value justifies that privilege.

If an API or server-side integration can solve the problem, I would prefer that over remote browser code. If browser execution is required, I would load it only on needed routes, minimize exposed data, consider a separate origin or sandboxed iframe, and restrict sources with CSP. SRI helps only when the script URL is immutable and the hash can be pinned.

For npm dependencies, I would review direct and transitive packages, license, maintainer health, release cadence, install scripts, known vulnerabilities and update process. Lockfiles and reproducible builds reduce surprise. Automated update PRs still need tests and review, not blind auto-merge.

The vendor should sit behind a small adapter with clear failure behavior. If analytics is blocked or down, critical banking journeys should continue. Network egress and telemetry should be monitored without sending PII.

The decision needs an exit plan. We should know how to disable the script quickly, identify affected builds, rotate credentials if needed and replace the integration later.

blocks.title: Practical design / code example
blocks.code:
<!-- Only when a pinned immutable asset is operationally possible -->
<script
  src="https://cdn.vendor.example/fraud-v3.2.1.js"
  integrity="sha384-BASE64_HASH"
  crossorigin="anonymous"
  defer>
</script>

<!-- Prefer route-limited loading or sandboxed iframe where feasible. -->
blocks.explanation: SRI verifies the fetched bytes against a pinned hash. It is not compatible with a vendor that mutates the same URL and it does not limit what trusted code can do.

blocks.title: Common weak answer
blocks.content: Assuming npm audit with zero current findings proves a dependency is safe, or loading a vendor script globally because integration is easier.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and production validation
blocks.content: Isolation may reduce vendor capability and increase integration work. Pinning improves control but requires a release process for updates. The cost is justified when the script can access sensitive workflows. Test vendor outage or blocking, CSP, network egress, dependency changes, reproducible builds and emergency disable or rollback.
keyPoints: Production validation: Test vendor outage/blocking, inspect CSP and network egress, scan dependency changes, verify reproducible builds and rehearse emergency disable/rollback.
Document the decision, assumptions, owner and rollback trigger so the architecture can be revisited when constraints change.

blocks.question: Does CSP make a trusted third-party script safe?
blocks.answer: No. CSP can restrict which scripts may load, but once an allowed script runs it generally has page privileges. The trust and data-access decision still remains.
blocks.explanation: CSP limits script sources, but it does not make an allowed script trustworthy.

title: Secure File Upload and Download
description: Protecting file workflows against malicious content, path tricks, authorization errors, active previews and data leakage.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Think of file upload as an untrusted-content pipeline, not a simple form post. The browser is useful for UX, but the trusted boundary starts at the server.

The safe shape is receive, validate, store under generated names, quarantine, scan or transform, then make available. Each step has its own state and failure mode.

Preview and download are separate security problems. A file that is safe to store may still be unsafe to render in your app origin, and a file that has an unpredictable URL still needs authorization.

The trade-off is friction and latency versus reduced blast radius. A senior design makes those states visible to users instead of weakening validation behind the scenes.
keyPoints: Treat client metadata and file content as untrusted; enforce server allowlists and limits.
Generate storage names and isolate files from the application web origin.
Quarantine and scan/process before availability.
Use safe previews or forced downloads; isolate active content.
Authorize every download and use short-lived scoped links.
Add quotas, resource limits, audit and malicious-file test cases.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: Customers upload KYC documents and later download them. How would you secure the entire browser-to-storage workflow?
blocks.answer:
I treat every upload as untrusted: the file, filename, extension, MIME type, and metadata. The browser can give quick feedback, but the server makes the real decision. The upload API checks authentication, tenant access, size limits, type allowlists, generated storage names, and content signatures such as magic bytes. Files should live outside the app web origin, usually in isolated object storage.

A successful upload means the file was received, not that it is safe. New files go into quarantine first. Malware scanning, parsing, and optional content disarm run with low privileges, timeouts, and resource limits because file parsers are a common attack surface. The UI should show states like uploaded, scanning, rejected, and available.

Preview needs its own design. I would not render active content inside the main app origin. For risky formats, use a transformed safe preview, sandboxing, a separate untrusted-content origin, strict content types, or a forced download with safe Content-Disposition. SVG, HTML, and original filenames need special care.

Downloads are authorized every time. A random object key is not access control. The backend verifies the current user, tenant, and document resource, then issues a short-lived scoped link or streams the file. Sensitive responses should avoid unsafe caching and should not reveal storage paths.

Availability matters too. Add quotas, rate limits, decompression-bomb limits, parser timeouts, cleanup for abandoned uploads, and audit logs for access. Tests should cover MIME/extension mismatch, polyglot files, path-like names, oversized archives, cross-tenant downloads, expired links, and scanner failures.

blocks.explanation: Checking only the file extension in Angular, saving the original filename under a public path and displaying the upload with `innerHTML` or an unsandboxed preview.

blocks.code:

Content-Type: multipart/form-data
# Server returns:
202 Accepted
{ "documentId": "doc_...", "status": "scanning" }

# Server authorizes current subject/resource, then issues short-lived URL.
blocks.explanation: `202 Accepted` communicates that transfer succeeded but security/business processing is still pending. The browser polls or subscribes to job status.

blocks.content: Only checking the extension in Angular, saving the original filename in a public path, and previewing it with innerHTML or no sandbox.

blocks.content: Strict allowlists and scanning can reject real user files and add delay. Keep the states clear, explain remediation, and tune rules by file purpose instead of weakening validation globally. Validate in production with test malware signatures, MIME mismatches, decompression bombs, parser timeouts, cross-tenant checks, cache headers, expired links, and audit completeness.

Document the decision, assumptions, owner and rollback trigger so the architecture can be revisited when constraints change.

blocks.question: Why should uploaded content use a separate origin?
blocks.answer: Serve uploaded content from a separate untrusted-content origin so active content cannot use the main app's cookies, storage, or DOM under same-origin rules. Pair that with safe content types, sandboxing, and forced downloads where needed.
blocks.explanation: Origin isolation limits the damage if a previewed file contains executable or browser-interpreted content.

title: Secrets, Runtime Configuration and Environment Separation
description: Keeping secrets server-side while delivering safe public configuration and preventing environment mix-ups.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
The key idea is simple: public clients cannot keep secrets. If JavaScript can read it, a user or attacker can read it too.

Runtime configuration is still useful, but only for public values. It lets the same artifact move through environments and makes rollback easier, as long as the app validates the config before using it.

Environment separation is an infrastructure and identity concern, not just a different Angular file. Redirect URIs, CORS, DNS, certificates, and backend authorization all need to agree.

Feature flags and config can guide UX, but they do not authorize access. The server must enforce capabilities independently.
keyPoints: Browser bundles and runtime config cannot contain secrets.
Separate public UI configuration from server-side credentials.
Use one immutable artifact with validated runtime config where operationally useful.
Constrain URLs/origins and fail clearly on invalid required config.
Enforce environment isolation through infrastructure and identity configuration.
Scan source and built assets; have rotation/revocation procedures for exposure.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: The team stores API keys and a client secret in Angular `environment.ts`. They also rebuild the app separately for DEV, TEST and PROD. What would you change?
blocks.answer:
Anything shipped to the browser is public. Angular environment files are build-time configuration, not secret storage. A user can inspect bundles, source maps, network calls, and runtime objects, so OAuth client secrets, private API keys, database credentials, and signing keys must stay on trusted servers or in a secret manager.

I would split configuration into public UI config and private server config. Public config can include API base URLs, non-secret client IDs, safe feature flags, telemetry endpoints, and build metadata. Sensitive values stay in the BFF or backend and are never returned to the frontend.

For environment promotion, one immutable frontend build with validated runtime config is often cleaner than rebuilding for DEV, TEST, and PROD. The runtime config should have a schema, version, cache policy, and clear failure behavior. If required config is wrong, the app should fail closed or show a maintenance state, not silently call a fallback production API.

Config must not become an injection point. Allowed origins and URL patterns should be constrained, and the config file should not allow arbitrary script, HTML, or endpoint changes. Environment separation also depends on DNS, certificates, CORS, OAuth redirects, deployment identity, and backend authorization.

CI should scan source and built assets for secrets. Source maps need a deliberate production policy. If a secret was exposed, rotate and revoke it; do not assume minification or obfuscation helped.

blocks.title: Practical design / code example
blocks.explanation: The public config is schema-validated and contains no credential that grants privilege. Server-side secrets never cross the browser boundary.

blocks.content: Obfuscating a secret, hiding it in a minified bundle, or fetching it after login and assuming users cannot inspect it.

blocks.content: Runtime config makes promotion and rollback easier, but it adds a startup dependency and needs schema validation, cache rules, and safe failure behavior. Building once per environment can be acceptable, but it still cannot make client-side secrets private. Validate with repo and asset scans, wrong-environment tests, config schema checks, and emergency credential rotation drills.

blocks.question: Is an OAuth `client_id` a secret?
blocks.answer: No. An OAuth client_id identifies the application and is normally public. A client secret proves a confidential client is trusted, so it must never be embedded in browser code.
blocks.explanation: Browser applications are public clients; they can present an ID but cannot safely hold a secret.

title: Privacy, PII, Logging and Data Minimization
description: Designing browser storage, telemetry, analytics, masking, export and retention around sensitive user data.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Privacy design starts with purpose. If the UI does not need a full sensitive value, do not send it to the UI. If observability does not need raw payloads, do not collect them.

Logs and analytics are data flows, not side notes. They need schemas, review, retention, access control, and tests just like APIs.

Storage is another risk surface. Browser storage can support useful recovery and offline behavior, but it also extends the lifetime of sensitive data on a device.

The practical goal is safe diagnosis: enough signals to debug production without creating a second database of private customer data.
keyPoints: Minimize fields delivered to the browser and mask/tokenize where full values are unnecessary.
Do not put full sensitive values in the DOM and merely hide them visually.
Use allowlisted typed telemetry; never log tokens, documents or arbitrary payloads.
Avoid persistent client storage for sensitive data unless a defined offline need exists.
Clear user data on logout/account/tenant switch and define retention.
Automate redaction tests and review analytics/session-replay data flows.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: A banking frontend handles Aadhaar/PAN data, account balances and uploaded statements. Product wants detailed analytics and full request/response logging. How would you respond?
blocks.answer:
I would push back on full request and response logging. A banking frontend should receive and emit only the data needed for the current purpose. Aadhaar, PAN, account numbers, balances, statements, and tokens should be minimized, masked, or tokenized whenever full values are not required. Hiding a value with CSS is not protection if the full value remains in the DOM or JavaScript memory.

Telemetry needs an allowlist. Events should contain route, build, operation code, duration, normalized error category, and correlation ID where useful. They should not contain tokens, credentials, full identity numbers, account numbers, document content, arbitrary request bodies, or user-entered text. Session replay and DOM capture need separate privacy and security review.

Client storage must be classified. Avoid persisting sensitive data unless there is a defined offline need. If IndexedDB is required, define retention, cleanup on logout and tenant switch, schema migration, device assumptions, and whether local encryption actually helps. A key available to the same JavaScript origin does not protect against XSS.

The UI should also prevent accidental leakage through autocomplete, clipboard behavior, downloads, browser cache, shared-device history, and exported files. Some workflows may need watermarking or audit, but backend authorization remains the real control.

Policy should become code. Use typed telemetry events, redact at source, add server-side filtering as a second layer, and automate tests that assert sensitive patterns never leave the browser.

blocks.title: Practical design / code example
blocks.explanation: A closed event schema prevents accidental spreading of arbitrary objects. Server-side ingestion should reject or redact unexpected fields as defense in depth.

blocks.title: Common weak answer
blocks.content: Logging full production API bodies temporarily, or masking a value on screen while leaving the complete identifier in DOM attributes and analytics events.

blocks.question: Does encrypting IndexedDB make sensitive data safe from XSS?
blocks.answer: Not against XSS if the decryption key is available to the same JavaScript origin. Malicious script can call the same decrypt path as the app. Encryption may help against some disk-theft scenarios, but it does not replace XSS prevention or data minimization.
blocks.explanation: Client-side encryption only helps when the attacker cannot also access the key or the decrypting code path.

title: State Management Strategy
description: Classifying local UI, URL, workflow and server state to avoid unnecessary global stores and duplicated truth.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
State management is mostly an ownership problem. The tool matters, but only after you know what kind of state you have and how long it should live.

Keep state at the smallest scope that satisfies the product need. Local component state is cheap. URL state is shareable. Feature state coordinates a workflow. Server state needs cache and invalidation rules.

Bugs usually come from duplicate writable copies. Prefer canonical state plus selectors and computed values.

A senior system makes state traceable. Developers should not need to search five services and three stores to understand one value.
keyPoints: Classify local UI, URL, feature workflow and remote server state before choosing a library.
Define owner, source of truth, lifetime, persistence and update authority for every shared state.
Compute derived values instead of storing mutable duplicates.
Use signals for synchronous local/derived state and RxJS for asynchronous streams/cancellation where appropriate.
Use a global/event store only when workflow complexity and team conventions justify it.
Scope and clear state according to route, user and tenant lifecycle.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: A large Angular application has component state, services with BehaviorSubjects, signals, NgRx and cached HTTP data. Nobody knows which source is authoritative. How would you simplify it?
blocks.answer:
I would stop arguing about libraries first and classify the state. Local UI state, such as an open panel or focused tab, belongs near the component. Shareable state, such as filters, sort, page, and selected report period, belongs in the URL. Feature workflow state can live in a feature-scoped store or service. Server data needs freshness, invalidation, and error rules, so it should be treated as remote state, not copied everywhere.

For every shared value, define the owner, source of truth, lifetime, persistence, serialization, and who can update it. Derived values should be computed, not stored as separate mutable copies. For example, selected transaction details can come from selectedId plus the entity cache.

Signals are a good fit for synchronous local and derived UI state. RxJS is still useful for async streams, cancellation, and composition. NgRx or another event store is valuable for complex workflows, auditability, and strong team conventions, but it should not be the default home for every form control and HTTP response.

I would migrate one confused feature at a time. Draw the state graph, remove duplicate sources, and add a facade so components depend on intents and selectors instead of storage mechanics. Scope feature stores to the route when possible, and clear user-specific state on logout or tenant change.

Success means a developer can answer three questions quickly: where does this value come from, who can change it, and when is it stale?

blocks.content: Putting every value into NgRx because the app is large, or keeping the same value in several stores and hoping subscriptions keep them synced.

blocks.question: When should URL state be preferred over a store?
blocks.answer: Use URL state when the value should survive refresh, work with back and forward navigation, be shareable or bookmarkable, or define the route identity. Filters, sort, page, and selected report period are common examples.
blocks.explanation: The URL is the browser's built-in persistence and navigation contract for user-visible view state.

title: Concurrent Requests and Race Conditions
description: Preventing stale reads, duplicate writes and out-of-order responses using cancellation, request identity and server concurrency.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Race conditions are not all the same. Reads often care about the user's latest intent. Writes care about whether a side effect happened.

For reads, cancellation and stale-response guards are usually enough. For writes, correctness must be defined by the server because the network can fail after the server commits.

Idempotency keys solve retry ambiguity for create operations. ETags or versions solve lost updates for edit operations.

Good UX represents uncertainty honestly. Unknown, pending, failed, conflicted, and confirmed are different states.
keyPoints: Use latest-intent-wins cancellation for search/typeahead reads.
Do not assume cancelled writes were not processed by the server.
Use server idempotency keys for retryable create operations.
Use ETag/version preconditions for conflicting updates.
Represent unknown outcome separately from confirmed failure.
Test reordered responses, double submit, timeout-after-commit and destroyed components.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: A user types `a`, then `angular`; the first request returns last and overwrites newer results. A double-click also creates two payments. How would you solve both?
blocks.answer:
Search and payment submit need different rules. Search is usually latest intent wins. Debounce the input, ignore equivalent queries, and cancel or ignore older requests when a newer query starts. In RxJS, switchMap expresses that policy; with fetch, use AbortController or a request sequence ID.

Writes are different because cancelling the browser subscription does not undo server work. For payment creation, disable accidental repeated clicks for UX, but rely on a server idempotency key for correctness. The same logical submit with the same key should return the same outcome instead of creating another payment.

Updates need conflict control. Send an ETag or version and let the server reject stale edits with a clear conflict response. That prevents two users, or two tabs, from silently overwriting each other.

The API contract should say which reads are latest-wins, which writes are idempotent, which operations can be retried, and what an unknown outcome looks like. A payment timeout is not the same as failure. The UI should query by operation ID before offering a new submit.

Client tests should reorder responses, delay acknowledgements, double-click submits, timeout after server commit, and destroy components before responses return. RxJS controls what the client observes; server idempotency controls side effects.

blocks.explanation: `switchMap` handles the read race. The idempotency key must be enforced and stored by the server for the create operation; generating a key only in the UI does not provide safety.

blocks.question: How would you handle a timeout after submitting a payment?
blocks.answer: Mark the payment outcome as unknown, then query the server by idempotency key or operation ID. Only allow a new logical submission after the original outcome is resolved; showing 'failed, try again' can create a duplicate.
blocks.explanation: A timeout tells you the browser did not receive an answer, not whether the server committed the payment.

title: Optimistic UI and Concurrency Control
description: Using optimistic updates safely with rollback, versioning, dependent caches and conflict UX.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Optimistic UI is a bet. It works when success is common, the change is reversible, and the user understands what happens if the bet fails.

The optimistic value must be tied to canonical state, versioning, and rollback. Otherwise different views drift apart.

Concurrency control still belongs in the server contract. Versions, ETags, conflict responses, and mutation IDs keep late responses from corrupting newer intent.

The teaching frame is to design a small state machine: pending, confirmed, failed, conflicted. Do not pretend the operation is done before the authority has accepted it.
keyPoints: Use optimistic UI only for high-success, reversible operations.
Patch the canonical entity and preserve the previous value for rollback.
Send ETag/version and reconcile the authoritative server response.
Sequence per-entity mutations so late responses cannot overwrite newer intent.
Represent pending, confirmed, failed and conflicted states explicitly.
Measure rollback/conflict rate and switch to pessimistic UX when risk is high.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: A user edits a transaction label and expects instant feedback, but the server may reject the change due to permissions or a concurrent edit. How would you implement the experience?
blocks.answer:
I use optimistic UI only when the action is likely to succeed, reversible, and low risk. Editing a transaction label can fit that model. Before sending the request, capture the previous canonical value and apply a pending version with a visible sync state. The optimistic change should update the shared entity source, not only the current card.

The mutation should include the entity version or ETag. If the server accepts the edit, its response becomes the new canonical state. If validation or authorization fails, roll back and show a specific message. If there is a version conflict, do not blindly overwrite the user's work; fetch the latest value and offer a merge or reapply flow if the field deserves it.

Rapid edits need ordering. Queue mutations per entity, collapse compatible changes, or tag requests with client mutation IDs so an older response cannot overwrite a newer local intent. Some actions, like deleting a regulated record or approving a payment, should stay pessimistic.

The UI should show pending, confirmed, failed, and conflicted states clearly. Screen readers should be informed of status changes without moving focus unexpectedly. Offline optimistic edits are a bigger design: they become an outbox and sync system, not a temporary patch.

I would test slow responses, rejections, conflicts, reordered acknowledgements, navigation away, and refresh. If rollback or conflict rates are high, the product is hiding too much uncertainty and should use a confirmed flow.

blocks.answer: Usually no. For a high-impact payment approval, I would show that the submission is pending, but the final approved status must come from the authoritative server after authorization, validation, and audit finish.
blocks.explanation: Optimism is a poor fit when a wrong temporary state has financial, legal, or audit impact.

title: Complex Forms, Drafts and Autosave
description: Architecting large workflows with validation layers, draft persistence, versioning, partial save and safe navigation.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Large forms are workflow systems. They need state, validation, draft storage, conflict handling, upload handling, and final command semantics.

Separate draft from submit. A draft can be incomplete and recoverable; a submit must be authoritative, idempotent, and fully validated.

Autosave is useful only if users understand what has been saved and where. If another device or stale tab edits the same draft, versioning must prevent silent data loss.

The design should protect both data integrity and user confidence: no hidden stale values, no fake saved state, and no last-write-wins surprise.
keyPoints: Decompose into typed section forms plus a workflow coordinator.
Separate immediate client validation from authoritative server validation.
Use structured field/global errors and clear hidden values when rules require it.
Autosave with debounce, draft versioning and visible sync/conflict states.
Use server drafts for cross-device continuation; treat local recovery according to sensitivity.
Make final submission an idempotent, fully validated command.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: A loan application has 15 sections, conditional fields, remote validation, attachments and autosave. Users may continue on another device. How would you design it?
blocks.answer:
I would not build this as one huge form component. The loan application is a workflow. Each section should own a typed sub-form and map to a draft command or view model. A coordinator manages step status, navigation, the server draft version, attachments, and final submission.

Validation has layers. Client validation gives quick feedback for required fields, formats, and simple rules. Remote checks, such as eligibility, should be debounced and cancelled when input changes. The backend still validates the full application and returns structured field and global errors. Hidden fields must be cleared when business rules say they no longer apply.

Autosave needs a clear contract. Save meaningful changes with debounce, include a draft version or ETag, and show saving, saved, offline, and conflict states. The server may accept incomplete drafts, but that is a different command from final submit.

Cross-device continuation requires server drafts. Local storage can be a short-lived recovery copy only if the data sensitivity allows it. Attachments should use independent resumable upload sessions linked to the draft, because they have different size, retry, and scanning behavior.

Final submission is a separate idempotent command. It validates all sections, locks or versions the draft, and returns an operation or result. Tests should cover conditional field clearing, async validation races, attachment failures, offline and reconnect, version conflicts, keyboard navigation, focus on error summaries, and submit retries.

blocks.answer: It depends on the draft contract. I often allow incomplete drafts, but the payload and server rules must clearly distinguish save draft from submit. Do not send a payload the server treats as a valid final application unless it really is valid.

title: Search and Typeahead at Scale
description: Designing debounced, cancellable, accessible search with ranking, caching, privacy and server limits.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Search at scale is a contract and load-management problem, not just a debounce problem. You need to define what can be searched, how much can be returned, and who owns ranking and authorization.

The browser is good at capturing intent. The backend or BFF is better at federation, security trimming, and protecting downstream services.

Latest-query-wins prevents stale results, but broad queries and high request rates still need limits, caching, and rate control.

A good typeahead is also an accessible widget. Keyboard, screen-reader announcements, focus behavior, and safe highlighting are part of the architecture.
keyPoints: Define query limits, ranking, result shape and latency before implementing UI operators.
Use a federated search service/BFF instead of uncontrolled browser fan-out.
Debounce, normalize, deduplicate and cancel obsolete reads.
Return safe match metadata; do not render untrusted highlight HTML.
Keep caches small, short-lived and partitioned by user/tenant.
Implement the WAI-ARIA combobox keyboard and announcement pattern.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: An enterprise global search queries customers, accounts and documents. Users type quickly, results arrive out of order and broad queries overload the backend. How would you design it?
blocks.answer:
I would define the search contract before tuning UI operators. The contract should state minimum query length, filters, result groups, ranking rules, cursor or page behavior, maximum results, and latency goals. The browser should not fan out uncontrolled requests to customer, account, and document services. A search API or BFF should own federation, security trimming, ranking, and limits.

The input stream should debounce, normalize whitespace, ignore equivalent queries, and cancel obsolete reads. The UI needs clear states: initial, loading, empty, partial, and error. Very short or broad queries can show recent items or ask for more characters instead of hitting the backend with expensive searches.

Results should return stable IDs and safe match metadata. If highlights are needed, return trusted fragments or structured ranges. Do not render raw HTML from the search index.

Caching should be small, short-lived, and partitioned by user and tenant. Recent exact queries can be cached briefly. Sensitive terms should not go into a shared persistent cache. Prefetching should wait until there is evidence that users are likely to select something.

Accessibility is part of the design. Use a proper combobox pattern with keyboard navigation, active descendant or managed focus, status announcements, IME support, and a stable input/listbox relationship. Measure keystroke-to-result p95, cancellation rate, backend query cost, partial failure, zero-result rate, and selection success.

blocks.question: How would you handle partial failure when document search is down but customer search works?
blocks.answer: Return grouped results with a status for each source. Show the customer results that are available and a clear retry or message for document search, unless the product requires the search to be all-or-nothing.
blocks.explanation: Partial results preserve useful work while making source-level failure visible to the user.

title: Offline and PWA Strategy
description: Defining offline journeys, local persistence, outbox synchronization, conflicts, service-worker updates and sensitive-data policy.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Offline design turns the browser into a small distributed system. It has local persistence, queued commands, conflict resolution, sync retries, and versioned app updates.

Service workers help with application resources. IndexedDB handles structured local data. Neither automatically gives you correct offline behavior.

The main pattern is outbox plus idempotent server commands. The user sees what is local, what is queued, what is syncing, and what the server has confirmed.

Offline is valuable when the journey is specific and high impact. Keeping the scope narrow makes security, support, and conflict handling manageable.
keyPoints: Define specific offline journeys and explicitly list online-only capabilities.
Use service workers for resources and IndexedDB for structured drafts/outbox.
Give every queued mutation a stable ID and server idempotency semantics.
Represent queued, syncing, conflicted and confirmed states honestly.
Design version conflicts, storage quota, schema migration and update lifecycle.
Apply a sensitive-data retention and managed-device threat model.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: Field agents must complete inspections with no network for several hours and sync later. How would you design the Angular PWA?
blocks.answer:
First, define the exact offline journeys. 'Works offline' is too broad. Field agents may need to open assigned inspections downloaded earlier, edit forms, attach small photos, and submit later. New assignment search, identity provisioning, and large reference updates may stay online-only.

The service worker should cache versioned app resources and selected reference data. Structured assignments, drafts, and an outbox of pending commands belong in IndexedDB, not localStorage. Each offline mutation needs a stable client operation ID and enough metadata for idempotent server processing.

Sync is a state machine. On reconnect, the app authenticates, sends queued commands in a safe order, retries with limits, and verifies server acknowledgements. The UI should show local-only, queued, syncing, conflicted, and confirmed states.

Conflicts need business rules. Versions can detect stale edits, but the product must decide whether to merge independent fields, ask the user, or keep both records. Attachments usually upload separately and then link to the inspection through stable IDs.

Security and lifecycle are central. Sensitive offline data needs retention rules, logout wipe behavior, device assumptions, and possibly managed-device controls. Storage quota and eviction must be handled before accepting offline work. Service-worker and IndexedDB migrations also need versioning so an app update does not strand pending work.

blocks.question: Can Background Sync be the only synchronization mechanism?
blocks.answer: No. Background Sync support and scheduling are not guaranteed, and users may reopen the app before it runs. Build normal foreground sync first, then treat background sync as an enhancement.

title: Real-Time Updates, Reconnects and Backpressure
description: Choosing polling, SSE or WebSockets and maintaining ordered, idempotent state under disconnects and event bursts.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Real-time systems need two designs: delivery and recovery. A stable socket in a demo is not enough.

Snapshot plus cursor is the core consistency pattern. The snapshot gives a known state; the event stream moves it forward. Versions and event IDs make duplicates and ordering problems manageable.

High-frequency data also needs rendering control. The browser should show the latest useful state, not spend all its time painting intermediate values.

Backpressure, authorization, reconnect, and observability are first-class parts of the architecture, not details to add after choosing WebSocket.
keyPoints: Choose polling, SSE or WebSocket from directionality and freshness requirements.
Use snapshot plus cursor/sequence and versioned idempotent events.
Reconnect with backoff and resync when event history is incomplete.
Coalesce/throttle UI updates; do not render every high-frequency event.
Monitor queue depth because standard WebSocket lacks backpressure.
Authorize subscriptions and manage one connection lifecycle centrally.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: A trading dashboard receives thousands of price and status events per second. Users see duplicates, missed changes after reconnect and browser freezes. How would you redesign it?
blocks.answer:
I would choose the transport from the communication need. Polling can be enough for low-frequency data. Server-Sent Events fit mostly server-to-client updates over HTTP. WebSockets fit bidirectional low-latency interaction. But the transport alone does not solve consistency or browser freezes.

The client should load a versioned snapshot, then subscribe from a cursor or sequence. Each event carries an event ID, entity ID, and version. That lets the client ignore duplicates, reject stale events, and apply updates idempotently.

Reconnect must be explicit. Resume from the last confirmed cursor if the server still has the event history. If the gap is too large or continuity cannot be proven, reload a canonical snapshot and then subscribe from that version. Use exponential backoff with jitter to avoid reconnect storms.

At thousands of events per second, do not render every message. Ingest events into a normalized in-memory model, coalesce multiple updates for the same entity, and publish UI changes at a bounded frame or time cadence. Some low-priority data can be sampled or aggregated. Standard WebSocket has no real backpressure, so monitor queue depth and processing rate.

Subscriptions must be authorized by user, tenant, and topic. Manage one connection lifecycle centrally instead of one socket per widget. Measure event lag, dropped or coalesced count, queue depth, reconnects, snapshot recovery, CPU, memory, and INP.

blocks.question: How do you guarantee no events are missed during reconnect?

title: Multi-Tab Synchronization
description: Coordinating logout, account switching, drafts, cache invalidation and singleton work across browser tabs.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Multi-tab behavior is distributed state inside one browser. Some messages are urgent security signals. Some are cache hints. Some data conflicts need authoritative versioning.

BroadcastChannel helps tabs coordinate, but it should not carry credentials or become the source of truth. Tabs can be suspended, closed, duplicated, or delayed.

For security context changes, clear first, then render. For shared editable data, use versions and conflict responses.

The right design combines quick local messaging with server validation and focus-time rechecks.
keyPoints: Synchronize security events immediately; treat cache hints separately from authoritative state.
Use BroadcastChannel/storage events for small same-origin messages, not credentials.
Clear caches and stop background resources before rendering a new account/tenant.
Use server versions for concurrent drafts instead of last-write-wins tab messaging.
Leader election is optional and must survive tab crashes/suspension.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: A user opens the application in three tabs, changes tenant in one, logs out in another and edits the same draft in two. How would you design consistent behavior?
blocks.answer:
I would classify what needs cross-tab sync. Logout and tenant changes are security events and should propagate immediately. Cache invalidation and feature flags can be eventual. Editing the same draft needs version conflict handling, not blind form copying between tabs.

BroadcastChannel is a good same-origin tool for small messages like SESSION_LOGOUT, TENANT_CHANGED, and ENTITY_INVALIDATED. Storage events can be a fallback. Messages should include a version, source tab ID, and minimal non-sensitive payload. They are coordination hints, not authorization.

When a tab receives logout, it should clear user state, stop streams and workers, cancel background work, and navigate to a safe signed-out screen. Tenant switching should partition or clear caches before rendering the new tenant so old data does not flash on screen.

Draft edits need server or IndexedDB versions. If two tabs save the same draft, both send If-Match or an equivalent version. One may get a conflict and must merge or reload. A channel can warn another tab, but the authoritative protection is versioning.

A leader tab can reduce duplicate polling or sockets, but it must handle crashes, suspension, and visibility changes. Often the complexity is not worth it unless connection cost is high. Since browser tabs can miss messages, each tab should also revalidate session and config on focus and API responses.

title: Normalized Data and Cross-View Consistency
description: Using entity identity, query membership and derived selectors to keep multiple views consistent without one massive store.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Normalized data keeps one local representation of an entity and lets many views reference it. That reduces stale duplicate copies.

Query membership is different from entity content. The customer record may change, and the list of IDs returned by a search may also need invalidation depending on filters and ranking.

Only normalize data with stable identity and reuse. Over-normalizing every payload creates mapping work without much benefit.

The hard parts are mutation propagation, partial versus full records, deletion, version ordering, tenant partitioning, and cache eviction.
keyPoints: Store shared entities once by stable ID and keep query membership separately.
Normalize only data with meaningful identity and cross-view reuse.
Update canonical mutation responses and invalidate membership/aggregates when semantics require it.
Use selectors/facades; components should not mutate entity maps directly.
Partition and evict caches by lifecycle and tenant/user.
Normalization solves duplicate local copies, not cross-user freshness by itself.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: The same customer appears in search results, a sidebar, a dashboard and an edit page. Updates frequently leave some views stale. How would you model the data?
blocks.answer:
I would separate entities from query results. Store each customer once by stable ID in a normalized cache. Store query results as ordered IDs plus filters, pagination, and freshness metadata. Components read through selectors or facades, so when the canonical customer changes, the search result, sidebar, dashboard, and edit page all see the same name or status.

Normalization is useful when data has real identity and appears in many places. It is not required for every response. A one-off report row with no meaningful identity can stay local to that query.

Mutation responses should return the canonical entity and version. The client updates that entity, then decides which query memberships or aggregates are affected. A display-name change may keep the same list membership. A region change may invalidate region-filtered lists. A delete should remove IDs from relevant queries.

Partial data needs an explicit merge rule. Search may return a small customer shape while the details page returns a full customer. Absence in a partial response should not erase known full fields. Version and completeness tracking, or separate view models, avoids that bug.

Components should not mutate entity maps directly. Cache entries should be partitioned by tenant and user, then evicted by lifecycle. Normalization fixes duplicate local copies; it does not by itself solve cross-user freshness, so polling or real-time updates may still be needed.

blocks.answer: Track field completeness or use separate view models and contracts. A partial search result should not overwrite known full detail fields with missing data. The merge policy must be explicit and version-aware.

title: Background Jobs, Progress and Notifications
description: Designing long-running exports, imports and calculations with idempotent submission, durable status and recovery.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Long-running work belongs on the server with a durable identity. The browser starts the work, observes it, and recovers it later.

The central pattern is command returns job ID, then status endpoint returns authoritative state. Real-time progress can improve UX, but polling/status fetch is the recovery backbone.

Progress must be honest and secure. Users need to know whether work is queued, running, done, failed, or expired, and they must only see their own jobs.

Idempotency protects retries and timeouts. Compatibility matters because jobs can span deployments.
keyPoints: Return a durable job ID quickly instead of holding one browser request open.
Use idempotent submission and an authoritative authorized status endpoint.
Persist recoverability across refresh/device and support polling or event updates.
Model explicit states and honest progress/stages.
Secure result download, retention, cancellation and audit.
Keep job contracts compatible across long processing and deployments.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: Generating a regulatory report can take 20 minutes. Today the browser keeps one HTTP request open and loses progress when the user refreshes. How would you redesign it?
blocks.answer:
I would model report generation as a durable server job, not a 20-minute browser request. The browser submits the report definition with an idempotency key. The server quickly returns 202 Accepted with a job ID and status URL. The job record stores owner, tenant, parameters, state, progress, timestamps, result metadata, and failure code.

The UI should be able to recover after refresh or from another device. Put the job ID in the route, recent-jobs state, or server-side user history. Progress can come from polling with backoff, SSE, WebSocket, or a mix. The status endpoint remains the source of truth.

Job states should be explicit: queued, running, succeeded, failed, cancel requested, cancelled, and expired. If exact progress is not known, show stages like queued, generating, packaging, and ready instead of a fake smooth percentage.

Downloads need the same security as other sensitive files. The status and result endpoints must authorize the current user and tenant. Results should have retention, expiry, short-lived links, and audit logs. Guessing a job ID must not expose another user's report.

Repeated submission with the same idempotency key should return the existing job. Jobs may outlive frontend deployments, so status and result contracts need compatibility. Notifications are useful, but loss of a push notification must not be the only recovery path.

title: Backend for Frontend (BFF)
description: Using a frontend-owned server boundary for token isolation, aggregation, view models and resilient downstream orchestration.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
A BFF is a security and experience boundary for a specific frontend. It is useful when the browser should not know tokens or service topology, or when the UI needs an aggregate shape that backend services do not expose.

It should be capability-focused, not a blind mirror of microservices. The BFF composes; domain services decide.

Because it sits on the critical path, resilience and observability matter: timeouts, partial failure, tracing, budgets, and compatibility for old frontend builds.

The design is healthy when it simplifies the client and improves security without becoming a new business monolith.
keyPoints: Introduce a BFF for token isolation, aggregation or frontend-specific contracts—not blind proxying.
Use server-side tokens and an opaque HttpOnly browser session with CSRF controls.
Keep authoritative domain logic in domain services.
Parallelize bounded downstream calls and represent partial failure explicitly.
Apply timeouts, safe retries, tracing and downstream request budgets.
Maintain backward compatibility for old frontend builds and measure end-to-end value.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: An Angular application calls 12 microservices directly, exposes service topology and stores OAuth tokens in the browser. When would you introduce a BFF and how would you keep it healthy?
blocks.answer:
I would introduce a BFF when it solves a real web problem: keeping OAuth tokens off the browser, reducing chatty calls, hiding unstable service topology, shaping frontend-specific view models, or centralizing web-session behavior. I would not add it as a one-to-one proxy for every downstream endpoint.

The browser should authenticate through the BFF and receive an opaque Secure HttpOnly session cookie. The BFF owns OAuth token handling, CSRF protection, correlation IDs, and web-channel policy. It calls downstream services with least-privileged credentials and returns contracts designed for the Angular app.

Aggregation should be bounded. Independent downstream calls can run in parallel, each with timeouts, request budgets, and clear optional-versus-required behavior. If one optional widget fails, the response can represent a partial failure instead of failing the whole page.

The boundary must stay clean. The BFF may compose, normalize, and reshape data, but authoritative business rules stay in domain services. Otherwise the team builds a second backend that other clients cannot reuse and that is hard to govern.

A healthy BFF has generated or validated downstream clients, safe retries only where allowed, request cancellation, cache rules, tracing from browser to service, and no sensitive payload logging. Measure whether it reduces browser request count, end-to-end p95, token exposure, and client complexity. If it only adds latency and another handoff, it is not helping.

blocks.answer: Possibly, when frontends have materially different interaction patterns, contracts, or security needs. Do not duplicate domain rules; shared domain services remain authoritative. One BFF can serve related web experiences when ownership and contracts align.
blocks.explanation: BFF boundaries should follow client needs and ownership, not an automatic one-BFF-per-app rule.

title: Micro-Frontend Architecture
description: Evaluating independent deployment, runtime composition, contracts, shared dependencies, identity, design system and failure isolation.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Micro-frontends are an organizational architecture. The main benefit is autonomy: teams can build, deploy, and support domains independently.

The cost is runtime composition. You now have remote loading, version compatibility, shared dependency choices, fallback behavior, observability, and local-development complexity.

Boundaries must be coarse and stable. Splitting by widget creates too much coordination and too many failure points.

The teaching test is simple: can one domain release and roll back without forcing unrelated teams to move? If not, the architecture is not delivering its main benefit.
keyPoints: Use micro-frontends for proven team/deployment autonomy, not ordinary modularity.
Align boundaries to stable business domains and route ownership.
Keep cross-frontend communication small and avoid a shared global mutable store.
Define runtime/version/shared-dependency and fallback policies.
Maintain design-system, identity and observability contracts.
Pilot one domain and prove independent release, rollback and support.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: Four business domains have separate teams and release calendars. Leadership asks for micro-frontends. How would you decide and design them?
blocks.answer:
I would first verify the need. Micro-frontends solve independent ownership and deployment constraints. They are not required for normal code modularity. If one release train and one team model works well, a modular monolith is cheaper.

If the need is real, boundaries should follow stable business domains, usually at route level. A shell owns top-level navigation, identity integration, route composition, shared telemetry, and a small design-system contract. Each domain owns its route subtree, tests, deployment, and production support.

Cross-frontend communication should stay small. Prefer URL and navigation state, versioned events for rare coordination, or backend workflows. A shared global mutable store turns the system into a distributed monolith.

Runtime integration needs clear policies: supported Angular/runtime versions, shared dependencies, duplicate dependency budget, remote loading timeout, CSP, fallback UI, compatibility, and rollback. Sharing everything couples teams; sharing nothing increases bundle size. A small stable platform layer is usually the right middle.

Design system, identity, and observability are product-level contracts. Every remote should be tagged with domain and build so incidents can be isolated. I would pilot one low-coupling domain and prove independent deploy, rollback, performance, and support before expanding.

blocks.question: How would you handle a remote failing to load?
blocks.answer: The shell should time out, show a domain-specific fallback with retry or support information, keep healthy domains navigable, and emit telemetry with shell and remote versions. One remote failure should not blank the whole app.
blocks.explanation: Runtime composition means a remote can fail independently, so the shell needs isolation and recovery behavior.

title: Design System at Scale
description: Building accessible tokens, components, patterns, documentation, governance, versioning and contribution workflows.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
A design system is shared product infrastructure. Its job is not only visual consistency; it also carries accessibility, interaction behavior, theming, documentation, and upgrade policy.

The best leverage comes from primitives and patterns used everywhere. If focus, errors, dialogs, and menus are correct in the system, every product team benefits.

Governance matters because teams will always have special cases. Good systems allow composition and contribution while protecting core semantics.

Adoption is earned through quality, migration help, and responsiveness, not just mandates.
keyPoints: Treat the design system as tokens, components, patterns, documentation and governance.
Build semantic, keyboard and focus behavior into primitives.
Use semantic design tokens and theme mappings that preserve contrast.
Expose intentional APIs instead of unrestricted internal CSS overrides.
Provide migration support, semantic versioning and contribution ownership.
Combine automated visual/a11y checks with manual testing of complex interactions.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: Eight squads use different buttons, dialogs, spacing and keyboard behavior. How would you create a design system that teams actually adopt?
blocks.answer:
I would treat the design system as a product, not a pile of components. It includes tokens, accessible primitives, composed components, interaction patterns, content guidance, documentation, test tooling, release policy, and contribution governance. Designers and engineers share ownership of the contract.

Start with high-use, high-risk basics: typography, spacing, color, focus, buttons, inputs, form errors, dialogs, menus, and tables. Native semantic HTML should be the default. ARIA fills gaps; it does not replace keyboard behavior or semantics.

Tokens should describe intent, such as surface, critical text, border, and focus indicator, instead of raw brand color names. Theme mappings can support tenants or brands, but they must preserve contrast, focus states, disabled states, and motion preferences.

Components should expose intentional APIs: slots, inputs, variants, and composition points. Unrestricted CSS overrides break accessibility and internal assumptions. When teams need something new, give them a documented contribution path rather than forcing hacks.

Adoption needs support: examples, design assets, generators, migration guides, codemods, semantic versioning, deprecation notes, and fast review. Automated unit, visual, and accessibility tests help, but manual keyboard and assistive-technology testing is still needed for complex patterns. Measure adoption, duplicate components, upgrade lag, accessibility defects, and delivery speed for common UI.

blocks.question: How would you handle a breaking accessibility fix?
blocks.answer: If the current behavior is inaccessible, correctness may require a breaking change. Document the impact, provide migration examples or codemods, test critical consumers, and roll it out as a clear versioned change instead of preserving the bad behavior forever.
blocks.explanation: Accessibility defects in shared primitives affect many users, so compatibility cannot always outweigh correctness.

title: CSR, SSR, Prerendering and Hydration Strategy
description: Choosing rendering per route based on SEO, first content, personalization, server cost, caching and interaction needs.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Rendering strategy is route-specific. Use prerendering for stable public content, SSR for dynamic public content when the value is clear, and CSR where interactivity and private data dominate.

SSR moves work to the server and adds cache privacy, deterministic rendering, hydration, and capacity concerns. It can improve first content while making the system harder to operate.

Hydration is a contract between server output and client code. If the two do not match, the user pays for errors, layout shifts, or extra work.

The right answer is hybrid and measured. Choose the simplest rendering mode that meets SEO, UX, security, and operational needs for that route.
keyPoints: Select CSR, SSR or prerendering per route and business need.
Use prerendering for stable public content and SSR for dynamic public/personalized content when justified.
Authenticated dashboards often remain CSR unless measured requirements support SSR.
Design browser-API guards, deterministic rendering, data transfer and private caching.
Use hydration/incremental hydration and defer deliberately, not automatically.
Measure field UX plus server capacity and cache cost.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: Your Angular product has public marketing pages, documentation and an authenticated analytics dashboard. Should the whole application use SSR?
blocks.answer:
I would choose rendering per route, not for the whole app by default. Public marketing and documentation pages benefit from crawlable HTML, fast first content, and CDN caching. If content is stable, prerendering may be enough. Dynamic public or personalized pages may justify SSR. An authenticated analytics dashboard often works fine as CSR unless measured first-render needs say otherwise.

SSR changes the architecture. Browser-only APIs need guards. Server-side data requests need authentication, timeouts, and private caching rules. Server and client output must be deterministic enough for hydration. Random values, time-dependent rendering, invalid HTML, and direct DOM manipulation can cause mismatches.

Hydration reuses server-rendered DOM instead of replacing it, which can improve visual stability. Route-level data transfer can prevent the browser from immediately repeating requests that the server already made. Personalized HTML must be marked private and varied correctly so one user's data never lands in a shared cache.

Heavy below-the-fold areas can use deferrable views. Incremental hydration can delay code and activation for selected regions while preserving initial content, but it should be applied deliberately.

The decision includes operating cost: render capacity, cache strategy, monitoring, deployment, and failure fallback. SSR is not automatically faster. Compare TTFB, LCP, INP, hydration errors, server cost, and cache hit ratio per route.

blocks.question: What causes hydration mismatch?
blocks.answer: Hydration mismatch happens when the server and client produce different DOM, often from browser-only data, random or time-dependent rendering, invalid HTML, or direct DOM changes before hydration. Make initial output deterministic and stay within supported hydration constraints.
blocks.explanation: Hydration depends on the client recognizing and reusing the DOM that the server already produced.

title: Feature Flags and Runtime Configuration
description: Separating deployment from release with safe defaults, ownership, targeting, testing, observability and cleanup.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Feature flags separate deploy from release. They let you expose a path gradually, watch it, and turn it off if needed.

A flag has a lifecycle. Without an owner and removal plan, temporary flags become permanent complexity.

Targeting must be stable and observable. Security and permission decisions belong on the server, even if the UI receives a public variation.

The hardest part is not adding the flag; it is testing both paths, handling rollback safely, and removing dead code after rollout.
keyPoints: Classify the flag, assign owner/removal date and define safe default/rollback.
Use stable deterministic targeting; do not randomize on each load.
Evaluate security/contract-affecting decisions on the server/BFF.
Flags shape release experience but never replace authorization.
Instrument variants and test both paths plus kill-switch behavior.
Remove completed flags and dead code promptly.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: You need to release a new payment flow gradually to employees, then 5%, 25% and 100% of customers, with an emergency kill switch. How would you design flags?
blocks.answer:
I would define the flag before writing code. This is a release flag, not a permanent permission rule. It needs an owner, creation date, removal date, safe default, rollback behavior, and a clear kill-switch path.

The assignment should be stable. Employees, tenant allowlists, and percentage rollout should use deterministic bucketing from a stable pseudonymous key. Random evaluation on every page load makes users switch experiences and corrupts experiment data.

If the flag affects API behavior, security, or contracts, evaluate it on the server or BFF and return the public variation needed by the UI. The frontend can shape experience, but it must not use a flag as authorization. The backend still enforces permissions.

Both paths need tests and telemetry. Events should include build, flag, and variant for success, error, and performance comparison, without logging sensitive targeting attributes. The kill switch needs a real degraded path; disabling a flow in the middle of an incompatible transaction can create a new incident.

Runtime config can load at bootstrap with schema validation, brief caching, and last-known-safe behavior if the config service is unavailable. Avoid many nested flags because the test matrix grows fast. After full rollout, remove the old code and delete the flag.

blocks.question: What is the difference between a feature flag and a permission?
blocks.answer: A feature flag controls whether a capability or version is released. A permission controls whether a subject is allowed to perform an action. A user can be in the released cohort and still lack permission, and the server must enforce that permission.
blocks.explanation: Flags manage rollout; permissions enforce authorization.

title: Frontend Deployment, Versioning and Rollback
description: Immutable releases, atomic publication, old-tab compatibility, canaries, telemetry and rapid recovery.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Frontend deployment has mixed-version clients by default. Some users have old tabs, old service workers, cached assets, or slow rollouts.

Immutable, content-hashed releases let each client load the chunks it expects. Keeping old assets avoids chunk-load failures.

API compatibility must cover the same window. Frontend rollback and backend rollback need to be planned together.

Safe release is measured by build-segmented telemetry and practiced rollback, not by hoping all users refresh at once.
keyPoints: Publish immutable content-hashed releases atomically.
Keep previous assets available for old tabs and lazy chunks.
Maintain API compatibility through the frontend rollout/rollback window.
Use canary/staged release and build-segmented health gates.
Detect version/chunk mismatch and refresh safely.
Practice rollback to a known artifact and coordinate service-worker/data-schema updates.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: A new frontend deployment causes chunk-load errors for users with old open tabs, while the backend has already removed an old response field. How would you redesign releases?
blocks.answer:
I would make frontend releases immutable and assume old clients stay open. Build assets should use content hashes, and deployment should publish a complete release atomically. The app shell can point to the new hashes, but old chunks must remain available for a grace period so old tabs can lazy-load what they started with.

The backend must stay compatible through the frontend rollout and rollback window. Use expand-and-contract changes: add the new field or behavior, deploy compatible clients, observe adoption, then remove the old contract only when old builds are no longer supported. Rollback is not safe if the backend already made a one-way breaking change.

Release should be staged when possible. Canary or progressive traffic needs health gates by frontend build: JavaScript errors, chunk failures, authentication errors, API errors, Core Web Vitals, and critical journey success. A build/version endpoint and visible support metadata make incidents easier to diagnose.

The app should detect chunk or version mismatch and offer a controlled refresh, preserving unsaved work where possible. Service-worker updates need coordination so the shell, chunks, and IndexedDB schema are not mixed incompatibly.

Rollback means repointing to a known immutable artifact, not rebuilding under pressure. Keep provenance, source maps, dependency records, and old assets long enough to support investigation and recovery.

blocks.question: How long should old assets remain?
blocks.answer: Keep old assets long enough to cover the supported open-tab, cache, and service-worker window based on real usage and risk. Use active-build telemetry and a defined policy, not an arbitrary one-hour rule.
