title: Monorepo and Shared Library Governance
description: Structuring packages, ownership, release/version strategy, dependency constraints and avoiding a shared-library monolith.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
A monorepo is a tooling choice, not automatically an architecture. It can support independent apps if boundaries and builds are governed well.

Shared code is expensive when its API is vague. The more consumers a library has, the more stable and owned its contract must be.

The project graph should drive CI. Affected-only work and deterministic caching keep the repo fast without pretending all changes are small.

Governance protects teams from accidental coupling: public entry points, dependency rules, owners, promotion rules, and cleanup of common dumping grounds.
keyPoints: A monorepo enables shared tooling and atomic changes but does not imply coupled deployment.
Categorize and own design-system, platform, domain and feature libraries.
Expose public entry points and enforce dependency tags/no deep imports.
Use affected builds and deterministic caching from the project graph.
Choose source/lockstep versus published semantic versioning by deployment needs.
Promote code to shared only with stable reuse, API and owner.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: Multiple Angular applications share UI, identity and utilities in a monorepo. Builds are slow and every shared change triggers all teams. How would you redesign it?
blocks.answer:
I would separate repository structure from runtime coupling. A monorepo can make refactoring, shared tooling, and atomic changes easier. It does not mean every app should depend on every shared package or deploy together.

Libraries need categories and owners: design system, platform and identity, telemetry, domain libraries, and feature code. Each library should expose a clear public entry point, dependency tags, and no deep imports. Large shared or utils packages should be split by responsibility or removed.

The build system should use the project graph for affected-only builds and tests. Deterministic local or remote caching helps when outputs are stable and secrets are excluded. A feature change should not rebuild unrelated applications. A central token or identity change may legitimately affect many consumers.

Versioning depends on deployment needs. Internal source libraries in a coordinated repo can use lockstep compatibility. Packages consumed by independent apps or other repos need semantic versioning, deprecation, release notes, and migration support.

Promotion to shared code should require stable reuse, a clear API, and an owner. Duplicating a small utility is often better than creating a common package nobody owns. Measure affected project count, cache hit rate, CI duration, shared-package change frequency, upgrade lag, and cross-team review dependencies.

blocks.question: When should a library be published outside the monorepo?
blocks.answer: Publish a library outside the monorepo when consumers deploy independently or live in other repositories and need a supported versioned contract. Publishing adds release, compatibility, and support work, so it should solve a real distribution need.

title: Error Handling and Resilience
description: Designing localized failure, retry policy, graceful degradation, correlation and recovery instead of global generic errors.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Good error handling preserves useful work while staying honest about uncertainty. Not every failure deserves the same UI.

Normalize errors centrally so features receive consistent categories, then let features decide recovery in context.

Retries are a tool, not a default. Safe reads can often retry. Non-idempotent writes require status reconciliation.

A resilient UI has explicit states for partial failure, empty data, stale data, unknown outcomes, and recovery paths.
keyPoints: Classify failure by scope, business impact and recoverability.
Localize optional widget failures; reserve full-page errors for missing critical context.
Normalize errors centrally but let features choose messages and recovery.
Retry only transient safe/idempotent operations with limits and jitter.
Treat write timeout as unknown outcome and reconcile by operation ID.
Provide safe correlation and distinguish empty, stale and error states.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: A dashboard depends on 20 APIs. One optional service fails, another times out and the user's payment submission returns an unknown outcome. How should the UI behave?
blocks.answer:
I would classify failures by scope, business impact, and recoverability. An optional widget failing should not blank the whole dashboard. Render the working parts, show a local error for the failed widget, and offer retry only when it is safe. If identity or required account context fails, the route may need a full-page recovery state.

The HTTP layer can normalize transport errors and server problem details into stable categories. It should not turn every 4xx or 5xx into a generic toast. The feature should choose the message and recovery action because it knows the business context.

Validation errors map to fields or summaries. Authorization errors should refresh permissions or context. Authentication expiry should follow a controlled reauth flow. Transient reads may retry with bounded backoff and jitter.

Writes need extra care. A timeout after payment submit does not prove failure. The UI should keep the idempotency key or operation ID, show an unknown or pending outcome, and query status before allowing another logical submission. Automatic retries are only for operations the API marks safe or idempotent.

Every user-visible failure should carry a safe support reference when useful. Telemetry should include route, build, operation, and normalized category, not sensitive payloads. Empty, stale, loading, and error are different states and should look different.

blocks.question: Should the frontend retry a 500 response?
blocks.answer: Only retry a 500 when the operation is safe or idempotent, the failure is likely transient, and the retry is bounded with backoff. A BFF may be the better layer. Never blindly retry validation errors, authorization errors, or non-idempotent writes.
blocks.explanation: Retries can heal transient failures, but they can also amplify outages or duplicate side effects.

title: Observability and Real User Monitoring
description: Connecting user journeys, browser errors, web vitals, API traces and release versions while controlling privacy and telemetry cost.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Frontend observability covers what the browser and user experience, not just what the server reports.

Useful signals need context: build, route, browser, device, region, and correlation. Without segmentation, averages hide the problem.

Telemetry is also a privacy and cost system. Use allowlisted schemas, sampling, low-cardinality dimensions, retention rules, and access control.

The goal is decision support: detect user impact, compare releases, trace failures across layers, and roll back quickly when needed.
keyPoints: Observe user journeys, browser runtime and resources—not only server uptime.
Include immutable build, route, browser/device and trace/correlation context.
Collect web vitals plus domain journey success/latency.
Use allowlisted schemas, sampling and low-cardinality dimensions.
Connect browser -> BFF -> service traces where practical and safe.
Alert on user impact and compare by release/canary.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: Production users report that 'the app is slow sometimes', but server dashboards look healthy. What frontend observability would you design?
blocks.answer:
I would instrument from the user's point of view. Server dashboards can be green while the browser fails to load a chunk, blocks the main thread, or receives data it cannot render. Collect JavaScript errors, unhandled promise rejections, chunk and resource failures, API latency and error categories, Core Web Vitals, and a few business journey timings like login, search, and payment completion.

Every event should include build, route, browser or device class, region, anonymous session or trace context, and correlation ID where available. It should exclude tokens, request bodies, full sensitive URLs, DOM content, and PII. High-cardinality values like raw user IDs should not be metric labels.

Browser-to-BFF tracing can use W3C trace context where CORS and security policy allow it. I would be cautious about depending entirely on one vendor or immature browser instrumentation. Stable internal event schemas make the data more portable.

Dashboards should compare builds and user segments. Alerts should focus on user impact: payment failure, login completion drop, p75 INP or LCP regression, and chunk-load errors. Alerting on every console error creates noise.

Source maps need secure storage and association with immutable builds. Release annotations, canary health gates, and privacy-safe breadcrumbs help answer the real questions: which users are affected, where time was spent, which dependency failed, and whether the latest release caused it.

blocks.content: More telemetry improves diagnosis, but adds bundle cost, network cost, privacy risk, and vendor cost. Instrument high-value signals, sample intelligently, and define retention and access. Validate that telemetry failure does not break the app, redaction works, build segments compare correctly, chunk/API errors are captured, and alerts are precise.

blocks.question: Would you use user ID as a metric label?
blocks.answer: No. User ID creates very high cardinality and privacy risk as a metric label. Use pseudonymous IDs only in approved sampled traces or logs, and aggregate metrics by bounded dimensions like build, route, browser family, and region.
blocks.explanation: Metric labels need low-cardinality, non-sensitive dimensions so monitoring stays useful, affordable, and privacy-safe.

title: Accessibility and Internationalization at Scale
description: Embedding semantic interaction, WCAG, focus, RTL, pluralization, locale formatting and translation workflows into architecture.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Accessibility and i18n scale best when built into shared primitives and team definition-of-done. Waiting until the end creates repeated defects.

Semantics, keyboard behavior, focus, names, and error relationships are part of component APIs. Translation, formatting, RTL, and text expansion are part of content and layout APIs.

Automation helps, but manual testing remains necessary for complex interactions and real assistive-technology behavior.

Sustainable delivery needs governance: reusable components, documented patterns, trained reviewers, preview environments, and measurable defects.
keyPoints: Build accessibility into the design system and definition-of-done.
Prefer native semantics; use ARIA patterns only when needed.
Combine automated checks with manual keyboard/screen-reader testing.
Use full localized messages with plural/select and locale formatting.
Use CSS logical properties and test RTL/text expansion.
Treat machine data and display locale separately and govern translation quality.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: An enterprise application must support WCAG 2.2 AA, keyboard-only users, screen readers, 12 languages and RTL. How would you make this sustainable across teams?
blocks.answer:
I would make accessibility and internationalization platform constraints, not final QA tasks. The design system should provide semantic primitives with keyboard behavior, visible focus, focus restoration, accessible names, error association, reduced-motion support, and tested responsive states. Teams should compose these primitives instead of rebuilding dialogs, menus, and grids.

Native HTML is the starting point. Use ARIA only when native semantics cannot express the pattern, and follow established interaction guidance. Automated checks in component and end-to-end tests catch many issues, but they do not prove usability. Critical journeys need manual keyboard, zoom, high-contrast, and screen-reader testing.

Localization should use stable message IDs and full messages, not concatenated fragments. The system must support plural rules, select rules, date, number, and currency formatting, and locale-specific calendars if required. CSS logical properties make RTL support practical without a second stylesheet.

Language and locale are separate from authorization and tenant. Server values should use machine formats, and display formatting should happen at the UI boundary. User-entered text should not be automatically translated. Missing translations need safe fallback, and rich translation strings should use a controlled system.

Governance matters across teams: acceptance criteria, reviewer training, design annotations, translation previews, and clear defect ownership. Measure automated violations, manual critical-flow results, untranslated strings, layout overflow, and real assistive-technology feedback.

blocks.question: How would you make a virtualized grid accessible?
blocks.answer: Prefer a proven accessible grid. Preserve logical row and column semantics, keyboard navigation, loading and position announcements, and focus behavior. Virtualization must not create unreachable focus, misleading row counts, or screen-reader confusion.
blocks.explanation: Virtualization removes DOM nodes, so the grid must still expose a coherent logical structure to keyboard and screen-reader users.

title: Frontend Testing Strategy for Enterprise Systems
description: Balancing unit, component, contract, integration, end-to-end, visual, accessibility, performance and production tests.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
A good testing strategy is a risk map. Different risks need different tests: unit tests for logic, component tests for behavior, contracts for API compatibility, E2E for cross-system confidence, and production telemetry for the unknowns.

Brittleness often comes from testing implementation details instead of user-visible behavior and stable contracts.

Mocks are useful, but they must not become fantasy APIs. Contract tests and malformed-data tests keep the frontend honest.

No pre-release suite covers every browser, network, and release state. Canarying, monitoring, and rollback complete the strategy.
keyPoints: Match test type to risk: unit logic, rendered component behavior, contracts and critical E2E journeys.
Validate API schemas/contracts instead of trusting hand-written mocks.
Test permissions, failures, races and malformed data—not only happy paths.
Use visual/a11y tests for shared design-system components.
Remove implementation-detail tests and treat flakiness as a defect.
Combine pre-release tests with canary observability and rollback.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: Your suite has 8,000 brittle unit tests but production defects still occur in API integration, permissions and browser behavior. How would you redesign testing?
blocks.answer:
I would redesign the suite around risk and contracts, not test count. Pure domain transformations, reducers, and formatting logic deserve fast unit tests. Components should be tested through rendered behavior: what the user sees, types, clicks, and hears. Feature tests should cover forms, state, routing, and network boundaries.

API mismatch needs schema and contract testing, not only frontend mocks that always return the expected shape. Consumer and producer checks should catch missing fields, changed enum values, error-shape changes, and backward-compatibility issues before deployment.

A smaller set of end-to-end tests should protect critical cross-system journeys: login, role-based access, payment creation, failure recovery, and file download. These tests need deterministic data, realistic environments, and clear ownership. They should not duplicate every validation branch covered in lower layers.

The design system needs visual regression and accessibility tests because one defect affects many screens. Add targeted browser and performance tests for high-risk routes. Security coverage should include dependency scanning, dangerous-sink rules, and API authorization tests; frontend E2E alone cannot prove backend authorization.

I would remove brittle tests that inspect private methods or snapshots with no business meaning. Test helpers should use stable roles, labels, and user actions. Network mocks should simulate delay, reordering, partial failure, and malformed data. Treat flakiness as a defect with an owner, not something to rerun forever.

Release confidence also comes from canaries, observability, and rollback. Track escaped defects, suite duration, flaky rate, and which layer caught each issue, then invest where defects still escape.

blocks.question: How many end-to-end tests should a project have?
blocks.answer: There is no fixed number. Have enough end-to-end tests to protect high-value cross-system journeys and deployment confidence, but not every branch. Use risk, runtime, flakiness, and defect history to decide.
blocks.explanation: E2E tests are expensive, so they should cover the journeys where integrated failure matters most.

title: Browser Compatibility and Progressive Enhancement
description: Designing capability detection, supported-browser policy, polyfills, graceful fallback and enterprise webview testing.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Compatibility is a policy plus an engineering system. First decide what is supported and why. Then design build targets, polyfills, feature detection, fallbacks, and tests around that policy.

Progressive enhancement lets modern browsers get better features without breaking the core workflow for supported older environments.

Feature detection is usually better than browser sniffing because browsers and webviews vary in surprising ways.

The balance is reach, security, bundle size, testing cost, and maintenance. Some features need a degraded path; some need a clear unsupported state.
keyPoints: Define and publish a supported-browser/security policy from real requirements.
Separate build syntax support, polyfills and runtime capability detection.
Use progressive enhancement for optional advanced APIs.
Encapsulate platform differences behind capability adapters.
Fail safely for security-critical unsupported behavior.
Test critical journeys on the supported matrix and use field telemetry.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: A modern feature works in current Chrome but fails in an older enterprise webview and on Safari. How would you design compatibility without freezing innovation?
blocks.answer:
I would start with a published support matrix based on users, contracts, accessibility, managed devices, and security support. Analytics help, but a small enterprise webview may still matter if it is contractually required. Unsupported versions should get a clear message or degraded path, not random failure.

Compatibility has several layers. Build targets handle JavaScript syntax. Polyfills can cover some standard APIs. CSS and Web APIs need runtime capability detection and fallbacks. User-agent checks are a last resort for known platform bugs, not the main strategy.

Progressive enhancement keeps the core task usable with broadly supported capabilities. A local export might use File System Access in supporting browsers and fall back to a server-generated download elsewhere. Background sync, notifications, and advanced media APIs should be optional enhancements.

Security-sensitive features should fail closed. If a browser cannot support a required secure behavior, do not silently use an unsafe fallback. Show a supported-browser message or a safer alternative workflow.

Encapsulate platform differences behind capability adapters so product components do not repeat browser branches. Test critical journeys on the supported matrix, including real enterprise webviews and Safari. Field telemetry should record safe browser, build, capability, and failure-category data. Dropping a browser is a product and security decision with evidence, notice, and migration guidance.

blocks.question: When is user-agent detection acceptable?
blocks.answer: Use user-agent detection only for narrow, documented workarounds to known browser bugs when feature detection cannot distinguish the behavior. It should have tests, an owner, and a removal condition.
blocks.explanation: User-agent detection is brittle, so it should be a targeted bug workaround rather than the main compatibility model.
